subsubtopic: EXHIBITION BRANCH DISMISSALS AND DEMOTIONS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave of the House to present a motion under Standing Order 43. My motion deals with a matter which I believe the House would like to have referred to the appropriate committee. I have tried to word the motion without incorporating any adjectives or argument in it. It relates to the announcement that some 15 public servants are to be dismissed from the exhibition branch of Information Canada, and another seven or so demoted, despite the fact that these people have obtained world recognition for the job they have done for Canada, their most recent achievements being at Expo '70.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett):
That the proposed dismissal of some 15 public servants, and the proposed demotion of several others, by the exhibition branch of Information Canada, be referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates for consideration and report, and that the said committee be asked to make its report to the House not later than February I, 1971.
The reason for suggesting that committee, Mr. Speaker, is that it is the committee to which matters relating to Information Canada and also matters relating to the Treasury Board are usually referred. We suggest no debate, and we hope the House will accept the motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bruce Howard (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):

speechtext:
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics reports that: A review of the answer of December 16, 1970 (page 2102 of Hansard) indicates that there may have been ambiguity regarding the interpretation of the term "average length of life". The figures quoted by DBS were for "average age at death" of those who died in 1969, this being their actual average length of life. DBS also routinely calculates various life table functions for the Canadian population and various sub-populations such as provincial and territorial. Two types of life tables are currently being produced: one, referred to as complete, are based on quinquennial censuses and are considered to be official; the other, referred to as abridged are based on population estimates and are prepared for analytical and research purposes. The life expectancy values at birth, sometimes referred to as the "average length of life", shown on the next page, are the latest available and, therefore, originate from abridged life tables. Life expectancy values are theoretical or expected and are based on the assumption that the population structure will not change and that the mortality experience on which the life table is based will remain constant during the life time of the cohort. The "average age at death" and the "life expectancy at birth" (average length of life) will be equal for a population where the births and deaths are equal for any period and where age specific mortality rates remain unchanged. The Canadian population structure and mortality patterns are changing; this is why the "average age at death" and "life expectancy at birth" are different. If it is assumed that the term "average length of life" means life expectancy at birth then the two tables attached show such figures for provinces and territories by sex.

REGULATIONS COVERING FLAMMABILITY OF MATERIALS USED IN AIRCRAFT COMPARTMENTS
speechtext:
1.	What regulations govern the flammability of fabrics and other materials used for the covering of seats in Canadian registered aircraft?
2.	Are all plastics used in the interiors of Canadian registered aircraft required to be non-flammable or fire resistant?

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: REGULATIONS COVERING FLAMMABILITY OF MATERIALS USED IN AIRCRAFT COMPARTMENTS
speechtext:
1. The applicable Canadian regulation for seat coverings in aircraft compartments occupied by either crew or passengers is specified in Part II, Chapter III, Paragraph 3.4.1, of the Department of Transport Engineering and Inspection Manual. For compartments where smoking is permitted the covering of furnishings must be at least flame resistant, (i.e., not susceptible to combustion to the point of propagating a flame after the ignition source is removed). All other compartments must be placarded against smoking. In addition to the foregoing, the following design requirements apply: (a) United States Federal Aviation Regulation 23, Paragraph 853, applicable to aircraft under 12,500 pounds specifies that all covering of furnishings in aircraft compartments must be at least flame resistant if smoking is allowed and flash resistant, (i.e., not susceptible to burning violently when ignited), if placarded against smoking, (b) United States Federal Aviation Regulation 25, Paragraph 853, applicable to aircraft over 12,500 pounds specifies all compartment materials must be self extinguishing after flame removal, i.e., flame resistant, (c) United Kingdom British Civil Air Regulations Section K4-3, Paragraph 6.1.2 for aircraft under 12,500 pounds and Section D4-3, Paragraph 9.2.2, for aircraft over 12,500 pounds requires all compartment materials to be at least flame resistant. The subject of flammability of fabrics has been the subject of discussions in ICAO. When the ICAO standard is finalized it will be adopted by Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the course of the past few months I believe the only words we have heard repeated as often as the recommendations of my colleagues and myself with regard to fighting unemployment have been the stand-pat responses of the ministers of this government. There is, however, one difference developing daily in this situation. These same recommendations that we have been making are being heard from an increasing number of Canadians, including an increasing number of economic experts, not just from the opposition benches. So, it is becoming more and more apparent that if the government continues to stand pat, it may well be standing alone in the short term.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As to the terrible unemployment faced by hundreds of thousands of Canadians this winter, admittedly there is limited action that can be taken at this date. However, let there be no doubt as to who is responsible for these hundreds of thousands of Canadians being in this position this winter.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Trudeau.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The stubbornness of this government in failing to act has been mainly responsible. At least let this government do what can be done at this stage this winter, and at least let it make the suggested changes with regard to unemployment insurance. Let us have an end to these stand-pat, complacent statements emanating from ministers of the Crown.
Looking a little further ahead, and recognizing the time factor involved in achieving a desirable level of employment in this country as well as the mess into which this government has put this country, the prime and major recommendation of the Progressive Conservative party is for the government to immediately implement selective cuts in taxation, including cuts in personal income tax of the order of 6 per cent or so.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brought in this budget on December 3, there was a general expectation that he would at least allow the 3 per cent surtax on personal and corporate income to expire as it was supposed to do, and as he originally stated it would. However, the minister did not allow this 3 per cent surtax to lapse, and the budget, with all its high blown phrases, became merely a means of extending the life of the surtax and in fact increasing taxes. In so far as the technical requirements, are concerned, the budget has no more reason for existing than this. Spokesmen for the government suggest that tax cuts would be inflationary. I do not for a moment subscribe to that philosophy under current circumstances, nor do many economists who are registering their objections to the present policies of the government. The Financial Times, for example, espouses a 10 per cent cut in personal income tax as well as cuts in corporate tax. An increasing number of economists and business people are calling for immediate tax cuts.
Let me say again that in present circumstances, far from a tax cut of this nature being inflationary, there is very good reason to believe that it would be anti-infla-
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
tionary. In fact, there is very good reason to believe that it might very well moderate the demands for wage and salary, increases which Canadians feel they need to offset the expected increases in the cost of living. I am not suggesting for a moment that we should abandon our concern about fighting inflation. I do not believe we have inflation licked. For example, I have been urging the government not to abandon sincere attempts to achieve voluntary wage and price restraints. The government got started on this program at a time when inflationary pressures were at their peak, the most difficult and very worst time to implement such a policy, and the program was in deep difficulty from the beginning.
The experience of other countries, notably West Germany, suggests that efforts to achieve successful economic guidelines and restraint policies, call it what you will, have a fair chance of success if they are based on consultation and co-operation among governments, business and labour rather than dictation from on high, and if they are instituted at a time when inflationary pressures are not too heavy. I say again that it seems obvious that rather than abandon efforts to achieve such a program at this time, this is the very time when the government should be redoubling its efforts to bring business and labour together to achieve a meaningful restraint program on a co-operative basis. Instead of this, the government has chosen to abandon its efforts. I hope nobody in the government is going to continue to give lectures to us on this side of the House about the importance of continuing the fight against inflation.
Another tax cut that could get a significant segment of our private sector moving ahead would be a substantial reduction or, preferably, the elimination altogether of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. This would give a very necessary and immediate stimulus to an entire job-creating construction industry. It is important, too, that if this government is going to fight unemployment effectively there must be some structure of responsibility. It is very difficult, looking from this side, to know who is in charge, or whether the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) is trying to spend one-third of his day fighting unemployment as well as handling immigration problems and problems in respect of wheat. From this side of the House there is no apparent co-ordination of government policy in respect of fighting unemployment, and it is urgent that someone be given the responsibility to fight unemployment rather than to have the divided responsibility we now see. Judging from the interest that he has shown so far, I hope that responsibility will not be given to the Minister of Finance.
The most optimistic forecast of Canada's economic growth for 1971, on the basis of the present budget arrangement, indicates that the highest expected growth rate will make no appreciable reduction in our present seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment. I have challenged the government a number of times to come clean and tell the country what its forecasts are in respect of unemployment for 1971. It has not accepted the challenge. Again this afternoon I sought this information and

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
I got an evasive answer. I repeat the challenge now, Mr. Speaker. I repeat the forecast, which I think is accurate on the basis of what I read, that unless additional and powerful stimulus is given to the growth of this economy, for this year unemployment, seasonally adjusted, will not be below 6 per cent.
During the past week I have been in the western part of this country and I should like to talk for a few moments about some of my impressions. At the outset of these remarks, I want to pay tribute to the personnel who staff the many agencies which are being pressed to the very limit in trying to serve the unemployed people in this country. I had the opportunity of meeting a number of these dedicated staff people, and I was impressed with their concern and the humane approach they are taking in trying to do their job. They are dealing, under pressure, with an abnormally high number of unemployed persons who would feel even more degraded by their circumstances were they being dealt with by case workers and counsellors who did not really care.
Some reports of my travels have given the impression that I was abusively greeted by a large number of people in Vancouver who, having no current eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits, were lined up to receive welfare assistance. That impression is inaccurate, and I think it is important that I clarify the details of this event. This has an important bearing on conditions in our country. Certainly, there were men in that line up who took the opportunity of my visit to speak out from anger to me. They are the men whose pride is hurting in a most unspeakable way. In addition to those men, and quite separate from them, there were a few vocal representatives of other groups who took advantage of the media coverage available to get their message across. All over the world today, people have become familiar with the techniques of abusive confrontation and the effectiveness of this tactic in gaining coverage. This effectiveness can hardly be minimized.
What concerns me about the nature of this kind of confrontation is that those indulging in it seem to have passed beyond the will or desire to discuss things. They feel that their only recourse and satisfaction lies in their organized ability to incite. I am, of course, troubled by this development because of the rejection and disillusionment that it represents. I caution the government, and I caution the people of Canada, not just to write off people in this state of mind as a disturbing nuisance. We must, to a large extent, endure some loud abuse and keep working at the problem.
By far the majority of the jobless Canadians I met in the line-ups at Vancouver and elsewhere have not reached that point of despair. They are trying to sustain their hope in the face of hopelessness. They are not the ones who have been making loud noises. Their anger and frustration is not visible on the surface. It is masked by whatever degree of pride they have left to display. To a casual observer, they would appear to have accepted their blows from a mismanaged and depressed economy with a reaction of sad resignation. But when you talk to
them, there is no mistaking that the same anger and frustration lies beneath the surface. They get their message across, too. It is delivered in a more restrained and quiet way, but the bitterness is there. They are shocked and frightened by what the government has made happen to them; and when they gather in welfare lines, hostels and manpower offices, I believe they are justified in directing bitter comment at anyone who sits in this parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration was the object of some expressions of this bitterness when he spoke in Vancouver last Friday evening. In his response, he conceded that his government's policies had been a cause of unemployment; but then, to his great discredit, he tried to run for cover and shift a substantial portion of the blame to industry and labour. He said that industry must "foresee shifting demands and plan accordingly for its manpower development".
No one will deny that this is a worthy aim. No businessman in this country will quarrel with the minister on that score. But, surely, such a gratuitous piece of advice is nothing short of contemptible when its intent is to mislead and to place blame on somebody else. Industry in this country did not deliberately create unemployment. Labour did not deliberately create unemployment and the unemployed certainly did not create it. This government created it and this government must answer for it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Prime Minister said that it did not worry him.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Certainly, as the minister indicates, industry is responsible for looking after its planning programs; but these do not exist in a vacuum. I remind the minister that for months and months I have been urging the removal of Ihe many uncertainties which the government has created in the Canadian economy. I have urged this because I know that industry cannot plan properly in a climate of uncertainty. Yet, in spite of all those months and months of cautioning and warning, the Minister of Finance has smugly refused to take any action. If we have reached a point now where industry is losing confidence in the good faith of this government, there certainly cannot be any doubt as to where the blame really lies. For the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to scold industry at this point and to ask it to act now without the government first doing its part, is more, Sir, than just putting the cart before the horse. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration is attempting to justify that kind of reverse arrangement after the Minister of Finance has wounded the horse and taken the wheels off the cart.
The prospect of a December budget brought fresh hope to many in the Canadian business community. Small businessmen in particular were hopeful of an indication that significant action would be taken by the government to stimulate the economy of this country. Their reaction to the budget which was actually presented by the Minister of Finance was, in many cases, a reaction of outrage. For many it meant that the Christmas message to a

January 18, 1971

further number of their employees would have to be one that would make them sick at heart. I talked with some of the jobless persons who got the bad news following the appearance of this so-called budget. They are not particularly mad at their employers who let them go. They are not blaming industry or labour for their situation. They know who has caused their jobs as well as their pride in being productive contributors to our Canadian society to be taken away. They know too that inflation is a bad thing and they want to be fair in assessing their treatment. Above all they know that they need hope to sustain them, and they know that this hope can only be offered by the government now scrapping this do-nothing budget and taking quick and effective action. That hope, Sir, will be necessary to sustain them over the long months that it will take the economy to recover, even if a tremendously stimulating beginning is made immediately. Yet, the government continues blindly to withhold the required actions.
Well over half a million Canadians right now are paying a deeply degrading price for this government's arrogance and economic incompetence. Those hundreds of thousands of Canadians have had to swallow their pride and take whatever assistance is available to them to provide food and shelter for another million and more innocent bystanders, the families who depend on them. Is this government now prepared to swallow some of its own false pride and take action? A growing body of respected economic experts says that it should. Industry says that it should; labour says that it should. Yet, I am afraid that because members in the opposition in this House say that it should, the prideful members of this prideful government may stubbornly continue on their ruthless course and be bent on saving political face at any cost.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance may continue to be proud of his one forecasting success. He smiles at us on television and lets us know that he was only a little bit out on forecasting the present dismal state of affairs in this country. He may continue to boast of the wonderful coming effects of his $2 billion turnaround and he may continue to gloat after achieving stellar price performance for the economy. But at what price, Mr. Speaker, and who is paying that price? It is not the Minister of Finance. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration may continue to tell us how it is "still reasonable to expect that the corner of unemployment has been turned." He says this, although well knowing we can expect a further 200,000 unemployed before the winter is over. The Minister of Manpower and Immigration may continue to lecture us in his patronizing way about "controlled recovery". But who is standing out in the cold and in need of more immediate recovery? It is not the Minister of Manpower and Immigration.
The Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp) may continue to treat with disdain and a verbal wrist slapping the warnings concerning potential unrest caused by unemployment that were expressed last week by both the Prime Minister of Quebec and his Minister of Labour.
The Budget-Mr. Stanfield
But who has to live and make a living in the province of Quebec? It is not the Acting Prime Minister. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) may continue to pride himself on the policies of his department at a point in time when most of the country is a designated area. However, who has to travel Canada's designated cities and countryside in search of work? Not the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) returns to this country, he may again give us his word that unemployment is now the number one priority of the government. He may again tell us how inflation has been licked and how he will not lose his nerve in the face of six per cent unemployment and higher. But who needs the nerve to face a family and financial obligations without a job? Not the Prime Minister.
Seme hon. Members: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that I fear anything I say will likely result in little action being taken by this prideful group of men who control and manipulate our economy. In characteristic style, I fear that they will complacently refuse any counsel but their own. There is every probability that they will stick by their mistake as long as people far removed from them are taking the lumps. Opposition argument and attempts at persuasion through debate seem to fall on deaf ears. All the arguments have been stated and all the warnings have been issued time and time again, but to no avail. My resolution to stick at it has been reinforced by the visits I have made this past week.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Any one who has seen what I have seen would be moved by the human beings involved in this terrible situation. I appeal to the members of the government to go out among the people to see for themselves the effects of what they have done and are continuing to do. I plead with them to do that, if pleading is what it takes to satisfy their egos. I cannot believe that the human hurt, anger, frustration and degradation that is being massively experienced all over this land would not penetrate even their insulated minds and stir them to take corrective action now. The action that is needed is clear. A mounting body of expert opinion supports this.
There is no time left to sit in the comfortable chairs of cabinet impressing each other with figures, graphs and computer type language. There is surely no time left to remain smug about a hopelessly inadequate budget. There is no time left to alibi and defend an indefensible mistake in economic planning. There is only time to honestly recognize the mistake and to start correcting it. That time, Mr. Speaker, is right now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say to the members of this House, particularly the members of

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
the government, that the unemployment crisis in Canada, which grows worse every month this winter, is economically unnecessary, morally indefensible and socially disastrous. I accuse the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) of deliberately and unnecessarily creating inhuman misery for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. I accuse them of cruel and heartless policies which sacrifice the welfare of Canadians on the altar of outdated and irrelevant economic policies in a modern and industrialized society.
I accuse this government of placing an impossible burden on the hard-pressed municipalities of Canada which now have to meet welfare costs beyond their means. I accuse this government of thoughtless disregard of the young people of this country, too many of whom are suffering the frustration and degradation of idleness and hopelessness. In short, I accuse them of creating conditions which cannot help but be an obstacle to orderly progress and will invite restless disorder and revolt against our society. What is most distasteful of all is the indecent smugness and complacency of the government in the face of this critical situation, a smugness and complacency that only arrogant men are capable of in a situation such as that which faces Canada today.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance complacently says there may be some difficulty now, but there is not a crisis. He says that everything is on the up and up. I say to him, tell it to the unemployed. Have the courage to tell it to the desperate young. Tell it to the men and women over the age of 40 who are out of work and who, in the best times, find it difficult to find a new job when they become unemployed. Tell it to the children of the unemployed who faced the Christmas holiday with doleful faces. Tell it to the hundreds of thousands of Canadian families who suffer from the policies which you so stupidly and callously introduced in this country.
There is no crisis for the Minister of Finance and his friends. Nor is there a crisis for hon. members of this House. However, there is a desperate crisis for hundreds of thousands of Canadian families and single men and women from one end of this land to the other. This situation, Mr. Speaker, is unforgivable in a country like Canada. We have riches which are almost beyond limit or description. Our people are industrious, loyal and proud. We have all the capacities to meet the legitimate needs of every section of this country. Instead of setting out single-mindedly to fight and eliminate poverty, this government deliberately set out to increase poverty in this country. It has succeeded. Instead of setting out to remove the glaring injustices and inequalities of our society, it adopted policies deliberately intended to increase those inequalities and injustices. It has succeeded.
With much fanfare, the Department of Regional and Economic Expansion was established. I do not think its policies will help Canada. Even those policies are incapable of being implemented in a general economic situation such as the Minister of Finance and the government have produced. This government, led by an insensitive techno-

crat, is the most reactionary and insensitive government this country has had for many years. I suggest that the unemployment situation in Canada is far worse than the unemployment figures show, and the figures are bad enough. Let me remind hon. members of them.
In December, 1970, there were 155,000 more people unemployed than there were a year ago in December, 1969. That represents an increase of 40 per cent in one year. In December, 1970, 62,000 more people were unemployed than in the preceding month, an increase in one month of some 14 per cent. But I suggest this is not a real description of the situation. The number of unemployed in Canada in December was not merely 538,000; anyone who reads the release from the Bureau of Statistics will notice that the labour force in Canada was reduced by 71,000 between November and December of last year, and the Bureau comments that this decrease is in excess of the usual seasonal contraction. What this technical language means is that many thousands of Canadians left the labour force in despair, young and old, male and female, and are no longer numbered among the labour force. The likelihood is that last month there were about 600,000 unemployed instead of 538,000.
It is certain that one month later the unemployment figure will reach about 600,000-that the actual number out of work is around 650,000 as we debate this subject today. It is certain that next month, and the month after that, unemployment in this country will go up to 700,000 to 800,000. The minister said the other day that this forecast is wrong, but I tell him that before the winter is out he will have to admit that not only are his policies wrong but that his understanding of the situation is limited, unimaginative and inadequate.
The range of unemployment in this country is not only the worst in the past ten years, it is worse than it was during the worst years of the depression. In this situation, the figures ought to be looked at again in order to see them from another angle. We have always drawn attention to this aspect but it is necessary to do so again. It is heartbreaking to note the number and percentage of the unemployed who are the youngest people in the labour force. No less than 19.7 per cent of the total of those unemployed are between the ages of 14 and 19. One in every five is younger than 19 years of age. Some 21 per cent of the unemployed are between the ages of 20 and 24. Taking these figures together, 40.5 per cent of the total number of unemployed are under 25 years of age.
What does this mean for our society? What does it mean for social conditions in a society where young people who leave schools and colleges to start out in life, perhaps to raise a family, are the ones who find themselves out of work, the ones who must face the despair and frustration of failure to find useful work to do? What does it mean in terms of the danger created for the orderly processes of society when circumstances such as these encourage young people to revolt, not only against their own condition of despair but against the society as a whole which has created those conditions? The danger is great, as has been shown in the Province of Quebec,
January 18, 1971

and it may be seen again not only in that province but in all parts of Canada.
The stupidity of the government's policy is greater even than I have described it when one thinks of what it has done to our total economy, and particularly to production. In 1970, the prevailing level of unemployment resulted in a loss to Canada's total production of about $5 billion. Between $5 billion and $6 billion were lost in the production of goods and services out of which $1 billion at least would have gone into the public treasuries to deal with situations which required to be dealt with. So, the stupid and insensitive policies of the government have produced havoc at both ends-havoc through the loss of productivity worth billions of dollars, and havoc through the loss of revenue available to federal, provincial and municipal treasuries.
When the government says this has been done to fight inflation it is talking not only nonsense, but criminal nonsense. I point out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that even his protege, Professor John Young, the chairman of the useless and almost dead Prices and Incomes Commission, admitted a couple of days ago that the price which has been paid in terms of unemployment in the fight against inflation has been far too high and is unacceptable. Dr. Young should have thought of that seven or eight months ago. We have not had any influence on the minister's thinking but had he tried he might have succeeded instead of failing in the task he undertook.
I say to hon. members that the unemployment situation and the state of our economy today surpass all the other problems which face this country and make it impossible to deal with those other problems. They make it impossible to deal, for example, with the threat of the FLQ in Quebec. They make it impossible to deal with pollution and the remodelling of our cities. How can this be done when there are hundreds of thousands of unemployed and a reduction in the production of wealth which could be channelled to these ends? They make it impossible for a government, which in any case has not the heart to do so, to improve the condition of the aged people, for hon. gentlemen opposite can now claim poverty even though this is the direct result of their own economic policy.
This government will go down in history as a government which instead of dealing with the social and economic needs of Canada arrogantly created a situation which it could use as an excuse for ignoring these needs. Unfortunately, in a situation of this kind, when a government has mismanaged the economy for a period of two years, it is not possible immediately to meet the unemployment crisis in any meaningful way. When the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) say to this House and to the people that there are no policies which could be immediately effective in reducing substantially the number of unemployed, they are right. But whose fault is this? Whose fault is it that no policies are available because of the time lag necessarily involved from the
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
point at which investment is made to the point at which it results in jobs? Whose fault is it that this time lag has been allowed to accumulate so that in January, 1971 very little can be done to reduce the number of unemployed which presently exists and which will increase in the months ahead? If the government had any consideration for the dignity and pride of human beings and was not so completely controlled by its technocratic concern with squares, computers, diagrams and excuses, then the government could do some things immediately in order to alleviate the condition of those who are suffering the misery of unemployment. I refer not so much to decreasing the number of unemployed but to alleviating their misery and hopelessness.
I understand that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey) will speak shortly in this debate. The minister has done a fair job in his department as head of labour relations and negotiation. He has frequently spoken with a voice that sounds almost progressive in its concern and sympathy for the condition of ordinary people. If this voice of concern is genuine and sincere, then the minister has an opportunity of proving it by introducing legislation in the House, either today or tomorrow, to provide for an immediate increase in unemployment insurance benefits to $100 a week. I suggest this step be taken on an emergency basis for the next three or four months. This will give the hundreds of thousands who are unemployed sufficient income immediately to live in dignity, even if their self-respect still remains hurt by having to be idle. If the minister's voice of concern and sympathy for the underdog is not only sincere but also courageous, then today or tomorrow he can introduce changes to the unemployment insurance regulations to extend the period for unemployment insurance benefits for those whose eligibility has already expired.
If the quiet and professorial Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) sincerely means some of the things he has been saying in the past two years, then he too can make an immediate contribution to alleviating the plight of many of our unemployed by changing the regulations governing manpower training and allowances. This would enable young people who have left school and college, who are therefore not in the labour force and have not been in the labour force for three years, to receive immediately the necessary retraining and allowances, thus providing them with some hope ahead, rather than the hopeless wandering across the country looking for work that is not available, in which they have been engaged. If the reason given by the manpower department for not taking this action is that the government has not provided them with sufficient funds to do so, then every member on the government side who has anything but partisan consideration for the unemployed ought to demand, along with every member of the opposition, that the government make more funds available to the manpower department in order that these improvements in manpower training and allowances be made immediately, at least for the winter months.
I am, of course, as concerned for the older unemployed as I am for the younger unemployed. Each time that the

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has sneeringly tried to suggest that we are asking for these improvements for the younger unemployed at the expense of ignoring the older unemployed-and he has done that on a number of occasions-I have resented it, though I have learned to expect this kind of irrelevant, smart-alec remark from the Prime Minister, particularly in regard to important matters with which he cannot deal consicientiously in any other way.
Although we are as concerned about the older unemployed as we are about the younger unemployed, the fact is that there are too many younger unemployed. Some 20 per cent of those without work are under 19 years of age. When you introduce young people like this into an atmosphere of idleness and despair, Mr. Speaker, you are making it impossible for them to make the kind of adjustment to life, the sort of integration with objective conditions, that is required to make them good and loyal citizens. Instead, you are cheating opportunities for degradation not only at their present stage of development but probably in their future development as well. You are creating opportunities for revolt against the entire democratic process.
It is, therefore, right that we should be concerned about these young unemployed, this 20 per cent that is under the age of 19. It is also right that the government should immediately make funds available to assist this group. I say that the Minister of Finance, who I think is listening to me even though from behind the curtain, has a duty immediately to make available funds to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in order that he on his part may make immediate changes to the regulations along the lines I have suggested.
As I say, the government can take immediate steps, not to reduce the number of unemployed but to reduce the misery of the unemployed, by making grants available- not loans but grants-to the municipalities so they can meet the increased cost of welfare now facing them. If this were done, two things would happen. First of all, the municipalities would not come under a burden that they cannot possibly bear and be forced to go to the provinces to press for things that reflect themselves in the provinces' accounts, thus making it much more difficult for the provinces to obtain the necessary funds. Second, and more importantly, it would enable the municipalities to liberalize their welfare requirements and make welfare available to more people. It would enable them perhaps to be a little more generous in the amount of welfare granted, increases they cannot presently bear on their own.
It is possible for the government to do at least three things that would have some effect on the number of unemployed in Canada. No one claims they would have a large effect, but as I said on December 12 last, I think it was, even reducing the number of unemployed by 50,000 or 100,000 is an act of decency that no one ought to ignore. This could be done if the government were immediately to undertake with the provinces and municipalities a great many more works than the Minister of Finance has provided for, particularly in the area
of social capital, such as the building of schools, hospitals, sewage plants and all the other things that improve the quality of life of our people.
When my leader asked today whether the Minister of Finance had changed his mind about removing the 3 per cent surcharge, I wish with all my heart that the minister's answer had been "Yes, I have changed my mind". The minister ought to remove this 3 per cent surcharge instead of extending it to the year 1971. To a large extent this 3 per cent surcharge on personal income tax-I am not so much concerned about the corporations-falls on the lower and lower middle income groups of this country which would use every penny of this 3 per cent tax to purchase goods and services and, therefore, immediately stimulate the economy.
Finally, I suggest the immediate removal of the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, especially for housing, though I warn the government that if it does this it should also take steps to make sure that the price of houses will go down and that the benefit of this reduction goes to the purchasers of houses instead of to real estate developers.
I must say I regard the Commonwealth conference as a very important conference. I hope with all my heart that our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will stand fast by the Canadian policy so far announced that we oppose the sale of arms by Britain to the despicable government of South Africa. But I say the moment that conference is ended, it is the duty of Canada's Prime Minister to come back home to take the necessary steps to improve the unemployment situation and end the suffering of the unemployed in this country. In view of this crisis, he ought not spend a single hour visiting anywhere else or amusing himself or doing anything in any other part of the world. His place is here to deal with a critical unemployment situation and the dangerous social situation which he and his government have created.
At the end of the war, 25 years ago, there was a great deal of discussion in Canada and throughout the world concerning the meaning of that war. Everywhere throughout the western world, after the defeat of the Nazis and Fascists, there was a determination in people's minds that the sacrifices of that war must result in a society which no longer suffered from the inequality, the misery and the unemployment which existed during the decade before the war broke out. At the end of that war, the Liberal party then in power produced a white paper in which the primary objective was a policy of full employment which must be introduced and maintained in Canada throughout the post-war period, said the Prime Minister and all his ministers. Like every promise of the party across the aisle, like every other social pretension of the Liberals throughout the history of this country, and like every other arrogant assumption of the rightness of that party throughout history, this promise of full employment which dates as far back as 1945 has been broken with heartless unconcern by this government as it
[Mr. Lewis.!
January 18, 1971

has been broken by other governments, both Conservative and Liberal, in the past.
I shall conclude by saying to hon. members that in one sense, with my social philosophy and social beliefs, I am not really surprised about what has happened in Canada. The total lack of public planning in our economy, the total reliance of this government on private enterprise to do the job for the Canadian people, the total failure to do anything about the allocation of investment in socially necessary areas, and the total unconcern of this government, the Liberal party and indeed the official opposition as well, about seeing to it that Canada's economy serves the needs of all the people of Canada and, in so far as it is possible, the needs of people in other parts of the world as well-these are the basic reasons for the failure of this government. The reliance of this government, and the reliance I suppose of the official opposition as well, on the large foreign-owned corporations in this country to be concerned with the welfare and future of Canada's economy in terms of human welfare and human wellbeing is responsible for the failure of the policies.
I say that, in addition to the specific suggestions I have made, the people of this country ought to demand a new approach, a new policy, greater public involvement in running the economy, greater public involvement in allocating investment and a determination to make full employment the first priority in any government policies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the present economic situation in Canada is alarming, even frightening and disturbing.
I just listened to the speeches delivered by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). The latter gave a brilliant account of the economic situation in Canada: 42 per cent of the unemployed are in Quebec, about 600,000 people are out of work in Canada; almost everywhere people do without the necessaries of life; the young are disturbed; heads of families over 40 are extremely concerned; the older ones are despondent; in short, misery hits an increasing number of citizens.
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Official Opposition as well as the hon. member for York South have very well described the present situation. However, there are solutions, and all hon. members, including the government members, know the wretched conditions in which too many citizens live.
Reference was made to misery among students, among the young who cannot find employment, among heads of families who lack the necessaries of life in their homes. All this is true, but there are reasons to that and the conditions tolerated by the present administration are exactly the same as those which prevailed in 1961, when Canada experienced the highest level of unemployment in its history. In fact, there were almost a million unemployed, while the Progressive Conservative government had 208 members and the highest majority ever held by a Canadian political party. And just the same, the fact
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
that there were a million unemployed doubtless contributed to the overthrow of the Diefenbaker government in 1962 or 1963.
Mr. Speaker, there are causes for this situation, and no action is being taken to eliminate them. Generally, the same causes produce the same effects. When the system is unrealistic, the whole population suffers.
Mr. Speaker, the first cause for the present situation is the government's failure to face its responsibilities.
Another cause is inflation, which has been talked about for the past two or three years. Two and a half years ago, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said: Because of inflation, I ask provinces, municipalities and school commissions to curtail all expenses. We will not improve services. We will put off projects of a national scope as well as the development of certain areas which are in trouble.
Mr. Speaker, hardly ten days ago, the same Prime minister was telling us: inflation? We have found it; it does not exist anymore. Yet, prices have remained the same and the number of unemployed has increased in the last month or two. Consequently, as regards this inflation we had two and a half years ago, the Prime minister was lying, or he is presently lying in the face of the Canadian people.
So, there was no inflation two and a half years ago and there is none presently. What Canada is suffering from right now is deflation, a lack of purchasing power in the hands of Canadian people to obtain products available in Canada. There is the problem that our country is facing.
Taxes are too high. We ask for a basic income tax exemption of $5,000 for married persons and from $2,500 to $3,000 for single persons. The government and the ministers laugh at us. This is absurd, they say.
Moreover, our financial system is stupid. Because of inflation and to fight it the chartered banks have been allowed to raise their interest rate from 6 to 9 or 10 per cent. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is aware of that. Either he was lying two years ago or he is lying to the Canadian people in the present crisis.
Mr. Speaker, although the Ralliement creditiste has been stigmatizing the stupidity of the financial system for 10, 15 and 20 years, our proposals are laughed at. We are told: The application of social credit would bring inflation. But inflation exists already and Canadians are asked to swallow that.
Mr. Speaker, the glut of goods today happens to be one of the causes of the unemployment situation in Canada.
The other day, I was pondering over statistics. Besides all the wages that are spent in Canada, our Canadian workers, from all social classes, owe the finance companies more than $12 billion. This is approximately half the amount of money now in circulation in Canada. We are told that to alleviate this situation, large projects will be implemented.
2500
January 18, 1971

The Budget-Mr. Caouette
To the employed workers of Vancouver, the Leader of the Official Opposition said recently: Gentlemen, let us reduce taxes to fight inflation. Let us reduce the tax of a poor fellow who has nothing in his pocket. How are we going to help him buy the products on the market? If he is not working, if he has no income, he does not pay taxes. What is the point in telling him that he will not pay any taxes? He is not paying any right now, because he is not earning enough money.
Mr. Speaker, those solutions are irrelevant, like poultices on wooden legs; the government refuses to face reality and then face the necessary reforms.
A few moments ago, I heard the Leader of the Opposition and the member for York South propose benefits of $100 a week for the unemployed. How are those who earn $65 a week going to react? They will be tempted to leave their job in order to receive $100 a week instead of $65, because they get less from their jobs than they would in unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a solution, and to take from those who have money in order to give to those who have none is not a solution either.
I said in English in Western Canada:

"taking away from the haves to give to the have-nots. In the end you will have all kinds of have-nots and no more haves in this country."

That seems to be the policy that is now applied. The intention is to tax those who have money to help those who do not have any. Even if we took one or two million dollars away from millionaires and the money were distributed among twenty million Canadians, it would mean a payment of ten cents to each one of them. But what would that achieve? Absolutely nothing.
The old age security pension has been increased by 42 cents a month. What a big increase!
Mr. Speaker, those are not solutions. The Opposition Leader was laughed at in Vancouver when he advocated tax reductions. What would that be worth to those who do not pay taxes or have not enough money to pay taxes? Nothing.
We are in favour of increasing unemployment benefits provided the employed are respected. If the employed are taxed so that money can be given to those who do not work and who thus receive more than those who earn their living, economic chaos will ensue.
We are aware of the present conditions. We know what are the causes and it is not by practising socialism that we will be in a position to restore the balance or respect the human being in the economic situation.
I have visited several socialist countries as I have already stated in the House. I have travelled in Russia. Highly placed people or union leaders in Russia work 46 hours a week. Everybody has a job. Full employment exists, that is true. Everybody works but the wages are

about half ours. In Russia, the monthly wages of an ordinary worker range from $45 to $55. The member for York South would not live there very long. What can one do with $45 to 55 a month? A Russian worker cannot buy a car that we pay $3,500 or $5,000 and which sells for $8,000 or $9,000 in Russia.
With $45 to $55 per month, one walks! This is exactly what happens.
Not television set, no radio, generalized poverty but within security. The freedom of the individual is entrusted to the state. The barber gives out a little ticket meaning: this belongs to the state. The taxi driver also works for the state.
Mr. Speaker, that is a system where security is gained at the expense of individual liberties. It is the same regime as that of my little dog: it has security, but in my home I hold the controls. It is exactly what I saw in Russia, Mr. Speaker.
Is this what we want in Canada? No. If achieving full employment as mentioned by the member for York South means that we will have to ask Canadian workers to accept salary cuts or a reduction in working hours so as to give jobs to everyone, I will have none of it. Two in the place of one with the salary of one only, that is the socialist solution which I will not accept.
The same reasoning could be applied to the two men standing besides a hole, each holding a small shovel, watching large trucks being loaded with a shovel-dredger. One says to the other: We are unemployed because a machine is used in our place. If that machine was not there, there would be jobs for 50 men like you and me, each with a small shovel. The other says: What for? The first answers: There would be work for more people. So, says the second man, 200 men with teaspoons could be used. Then, the same work would be done, the same trucks would be loaded, but 200 men would have jobs.
Mr. Speaker, the press people may laugh but that is the solution they have been advocating in their papers for years and years. That is socialism, in all its splendour.
Not only in Russia, but in Czechcoslovakia also, it is the same.
It is often said: What a splendid country Sweden is! Yes, it is a spendid country. Here is an example. I arrive there one day and I take a bus at a street corner. I note, it is true, that everyone is working, but freedom is in the hands of the state, and that of the individual is not respected.
Four people were at work there-a New Democratic Party member is starting to "sound off" a little because his party has no solution to offer-four employees running one bus: one selling tickets, another perforating them, a third driving the vehicle and a last one supervising the other three checking on whether they were doing their job properly. That was in Sweden.
Whether New Democratic Party members like it or not, it must be pointed out that during the big economic
January 18, 1971

depression and immediately after the war the Canadian province with the greatest number of unemployed was still Saskatchewan, under a Socialist government. For 17 years, people were leaving Saskatchewan for Alberta or British Columbia because they could no longer live in Saskatchewan with a Socialist government.
Mr. Speaker, is that the kind of government we want in Canada? No. What, then, do we recommend? We have a solution. It does not involve creating jobs, but consuming Canadian products. First of all, let us set up the consumer goods system in order to consume what is being produced, because there is too much of everything. Would it be advisable for the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) to grant a $200 million subsidy tomorrow for the construction of a new shoe factory, when we already have too many shoes?
Is the clothing industry any better off? There is an overabundance of shoes, clothes, TV and radio sets, automobiles. Shall we subsidize the automobile industry? No. Because there are already too many cars and we would not know what to do with them.
In Western Canada, there are too many tractors, there is too much wheat and milk. We penalized milk producers because they were producing too much milk; they must not exceed their quotas. There is a glut of corn and potatoes in New Brunswick, in Prince Edward Island and in Manitoba. There is also a glut of butter and eggs!
The Prime Minister went to New Zealand and he said there: We will buy your eggs. Canadian farmers are not even able to sell theirs! There are too many chickens. Even now there is quarelling going on from Manitoba to Quebec because Quebec chickens are being dumped in Manitoba and Manitoba potatoes are being dumped in Ontario. The time of day is being spent dumping. The whole population of Canada is being dumped with that crazy system.
There is too much meat, beef, pork and chicken. What is lacking, then? New funds, new credits from the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, but not to build new plants or expand old ones to produce more: we already have too much.
What is lacking, Mr. Speaker? Purchasing power that corresponds to our production. What do the Creditistes suggest? We will be very specific in our proposal.
First of all, the Bank of Canada must be used-not the New York Bank, but the Bank of Canada-in order to use our credit and not American credit. A domstic economic organization must be set up in Canada without jeopardizing external trade. Americans are not interested in knowing what is the colour of the Canadian dollar or Canadian credit but rather what they can purchase in our country for one Canadian dollar. If we offer more goods for one dollar, they will be interested in coming here. Our dollars are not in circulation in the United States, in Sweden or in England. It is so true that if we go in the Southern United States and we show people a Canadian dollar, they wonder whose likeness appears on it. They wonder what currency it is, whether it comes
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
from Mexico. It looks like a Mexican peso. Even 25c. coins are not accepted by cigarette machines in the United States.
There are some solutions. They are not those suggested by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, who made a statement during the weekend.
Here is what one can read in today's Le Droit:
Marchand outlines federal policy Measures against unemployment
The Canadian Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, Hon. Jean Marchand, has said, over the weekend, that it was "really unfair" to claim that Ottawa is doing nothing to control unemployment.
We try something that fails, but at least we do something.
Speaking during the telecast "Les affaires de 1'Etat" of the CBC French network, Mr. Marchand has submitted that for more than one and a half years, the federal government has waged a systematic battle against unemployment in Canada.
Now that we have fought, the number of unemployed has increased by at least 100,000 during December. According to Premier Bourrassa's program, in Quebec,
100.000	jobs were to be created. Instead, we have had
100.000	layoffs; that is not at all what had been recommended. And the minister goes to Quebec and tells the people: "It's coming, we have been working on it for the past 18 months. Results are forthcoming. But in the meantime, things go from bad to worse. There is no solution because we do not have any money.
The minister also said, and I quote from the newspaper Le Droit.
said that during the past 18 months the government has injected well over $2 billion in our economy.
Injected where? Into what? Into the construction of plants that will manufacture goods that people cannot afford to buy. Into assisting people who happen to be in a precarious financial situation? This we did. V^e prevented people from toppling over because their products could not be sold. Then we injected into the economy billions of dollars which failed to allow the consumer to buy these goods, which will prolong the consumer's destitution and maintain these industries in operation for 18 months. Eventually, the minister will have injected those $2 billion to maintain the industries in operation but the Canadian consumer is ignored completely. The government forgets about him. Old age pensions are increased by 42 cents a month. The minister went on as follows:
There was an expansionist taxation policy_
Let us ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) whether there was an expansionist taxation policy. In what area? In what sense? Where has the field of taxation expanded? The provinces are always at a loss against Ottawa and all of them blame Ottawa without exception for this taxation system which prevents them from developing. The minister knows that.
-and an expansionist monetary policy,-
-with debts, of course. It was not credit granted by the Bank of Canada, but credit begged on bended knees

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Caouette
in New York and Washington, in order to get permission to develop our country, Canada. Then, we are surprised to hear people say: Our economy is controlled by Americans. Of course, and it is normal since they finance the development while we could use our financial institution, the Bank of Canada. I dare the Minister of Finance to deny this. We, in Parliament, have the power to use the Bank of Canada and to make it serve the provinces, municipalities and school boards to allow them to expand through interest-free loans such as those that are given India, China and other countries.
Instead of using the Bank of Canada, we make it a branch of chartered banks in Canada and then we go to New York and Washington and beg for money to develop the far North and the province of Quebec. We go there to borrow $75 million at a rate of 8f per cent during 25 years for the implementation of a Hydro-Quebec project in the province of Quebec. In 25 years we will have paid $200 million in interest alone and we will still owe the $75 million we have just borrowed. Mr. Bourrassa, who succeeded Mr. Bertrand, is to blame for that. Bitten by a dog or bitten by a bitch, what is the difference, Mr. Speaker? It is the same thing. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion said also, and I quote:
Mr. Marchand mentioned the selective measures used by the government to fight unemployment with regard to the old people-
How nice: the old people and the unemployed. But what marvellous thing were done for the unemployed? One single day does not go by without our receiving 25, 30 or 50 phone calls from people without work who are treated like intruders at unemployment offices. Their cases are not always solved by the regional offices; they are referred to Montreal where there are electronic machines. And when these do not work, the unemployed starve at the other end.
Back to the quotation:
_family heads; in areas whose growth is inadequate-
Talk about welfare! Big families are asked to live on $160, $165 and $170 a month. Has the minister a formula look after the needs of a family of seven with $175 per month? I would then listen to the minister and to the government. I continue to quote:
-in areas whose growth is inadequate-
I mentioned that a while ago; they are especially those which are helped.
shipyards, footwear industries, etc.
We have too large stocks of footwear. I will speak to The Manufacturers' Association next Monday in Sainte-Adele at the Chanteclerc Hotel. I invite the minister to come with me so that we may discuss together problems of the footwear and textile industries, of gold mines and the entire Canadian production. The newspaper also reports as follows:
The minister has emphasized that under the new plan ... the province of Quebec is now a designated area-

In fact, that is a beautiful quality.
-which will enable it to get grants amounting to $100 million in the next few years.
$100 million are taken from other Canadian provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to be too long, but I wish to say in closing that the solution advocated by the Credi-tistes is as follows: first, instead of saying "increase the rate of benefits", we recommend the immediate distribution of a national dividend to each Canadian citizen, whether employed or unemployed. To make a distinction between the one who works and the one who does not there will be the difference of a salary, but every human person, the unemployed and the one on welfare alike, should be provided with the security of a guaranteed vital minimum. That is what is called the guaranteed annual income in scientific terms, such as those used by the government. We advocate payment of an old age pension of $150 per month, not 42 cents per day or $135 monthly. Such a pension would also be payable at 60, because at that age one is too old for family allowances and too young for the old age pension. The older person would receive a pension of $150 at 60 and his spouse, regardless of age, would also receive the old age pension. This would create purchasing power and enable people to acquire goods. Instead of doing away with family allowances or reducing them, they should be adjusted to the cost of living and family allowances should be increased, with the money coming from the Bank of Canada and not from my pockets. What we have in our pockets we need. So, why take it away from us?
The answer is to seek the money where credit is created, that is at the Bank of Canada. Why go to New York to ask Mr. Nixon permission to support my child, back home, in Abitibi? President Nixon never saw Abitibi in his fife but the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion did, as well as the Minister of Finance. As for me, I go there fairly regularly.
Mr. Speaker, why not use the Bank of Canada to grant interest free loans to the provinces, municipalities and school boards, in order to allow them to develop normally.
Then, a presalary should be paid to students. I am not the one who advocated this idea, it comes from United States. Rather than have to ask $2 to his father who earns $75 a week and has five or six children to support, the student should receive a presalary and therefore be saved any embarrassment. Instead of letting him fooling around as he does now, without knowing where to turn, we must organize his spare time, give him some guidance and guarantee him his right to live in our society.
Why do young people rebel? Because they are refused the right to live within our society. Since they cannot find a place for themselves in that society, they attempt to destroy it. That is precisely what is happening.
But where would this presalary paid to students come from? Out of my pockets? Certainly not, because I need what I have in my pockets. I am sure the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) also needs what he has in his pockets.
January 18, 1971

However, there is no reason why we should not get the credits required from the Bank of Canada, based on Canadian production, not on the moon or the planet Mars. Canadian production reached $77 billion this year, whereas we receive $55 billion. Economists object to the Creditiste theory, claiming that there must be a depreciation of production for income tax purposes.
That is quite obvious. The man who does a lot of business will try to effect a maximum depreciation in order to pay a minimum of income tax. That is obvious. Everyone understands, and so does the minister. But what does the depreciation result in? In the present surplus, surplus goods now standing on shop shelves.
And to prove it, you see, all our national income has been spent. Stores are still full of goods. Plants are operating on a slow-down basis because the goods they manufacture cannot be sold and this situation creates unemployment. There is the problem.
Then, where does depreciation hit us? On the shelves of our stores. The Bank of Canada must be used to distribute purchasing power by means of a compensated discount, or by a national dividend that would permit the consumer to buy the goods piled up in our stores.
Once the shelves in our stores become empty, the plants resume operation and unemployed workers are put to work. Then, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion will be extremely pleased to see the Canadian consumer back to work.
Instead of subsidizing plants, let us subsidize consumers; they will put the plants back into operation when they buy the goods manufactured by the plants. We will then experience a sound economic system fit for human beings and in which every Canadian citizen will feel secure in his own country while preserving in its integrity his own personal freedom. That is what we have been striving to accomplish for so many years.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take advantage of the kindness of my colleagues.
That is the solution the Creditistes have been proposing for many years. I will be told-as I was on Sunday afternoon on channel 10-that this has never been tested anywhere. That is true, but things are going wrong everywhere!
If our solutions would be tested somewhere things would perhaps go better again. If they are not good, then
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
we simply discard them. We are convinced that the present system is not good, but the Canadian people have to live with it.
Some citizens still praise that system. If prosperity is brought to one area, nobody looks elsewhere where there is misery. Mr. Speaker, the solution to the present problem rests with the economic system. We must resort to an economic solution in order to safeguard personal freedom and personal security. This is what the Creditistes wish for.
I appeal to the Minister of Finance, to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, to the Prime Minister of Canada who is now travelling in India, Pakistan and Singapour, in short I appeal to the present government, for a more human economic system, a system which will enable young people to develop, to understand things better, to get training, to choose a course in life, and which will give Canadian fathers and mothers the assurance of raising a normal family in a normal system.
And for our older people, the assurance of security and independence for their later years. This what the Creditistes have been urging for quite a long time without any partisan spirit. Let the Liberal Party take on these concepts and I am sure that my colleagues from the Ralliement creditiste and myself will fully support it in giving the people of Canada a political system that will ensure security and freedom for everyone.

Mr. Speaker, I participated in a similar debate on the budget a few weeks ago, probably on an amendment of the New Democratic Party. When listening to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and other speakers, there was something all too familiar about their participation today. In the weeks since the budget was first introduced into the House, none of the speakers from whom we heard this afternoon have been able to find any fresh material.
I presume that the purpose of the debate, asked for by the official opposition, is to justify the fact that the Leader of Opposition had suddenly discovered unemployment and the problems which unemployment brings to the less fortunate people of this country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
