speechtext:
I suspect the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) will be unemployed following that convention, but he will always be welcome in the House. He has the audacity to speak about ordinary people as if he were an ordinary person, and therefore, should know something about the subject.

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
One of the themes, which has permeated the debate, certainly the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition, is a concern with the plight of the unemployed. I would be much too partisan if I pretended that his concern for the unemployed of this country were superficial or new found. The record of the Leader of the Opposition when he was the premier of Nova Scotia indicates that he does have a social conscience and does care for the people. I take issue with the Leader of the Opposition and others who presume that concern for the unemployed people of this country is limited to the Opposition. This is not so, Mr. Speaker. We do not need a lecture on what unemployment does to a country. No one on this side of the House is happy with the rate of unemployment.
Some speakers have said that we must look back to the great depression to remember unemployment. We do not have to look back that far, Mr. Speaker. We need only go back 10, 11 or 12 years in order to remember unemployment in this country. Some newer members in this chamber do not remember the debates of 1962 and 1963. I wish to deal with the rate of unemployment in those years, but not to be highly partisan because this is not a partisan debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member said "oh, no". I wrote down some of the adjectives he used, such as stupid, arrogant. He suppressed the hope that the Prime Minister would not stay away to amuse himself. The hon. member does not know how to be nonpartisan. He does not think this subject is worthy of being nonpartisan. He is now in the unfavourable position where everything he says in the House of Commons will have some bearing on the events that will take place in the months to come. He is on the horns of a dilemma. His position is not unlike the position adopted by his party toward the problems of Quebec. At one time, they could hide behind the communications wall. Now, there is instantaneous communication and, events in Quebec can be reported ten minutes later in British Columbia.
In 1958, when the Conservatives were in power, the national rate of unemployment in this country was seven per cent. That was not in the hungry thirties, it was only 12 years ago. In 1959, the rate of unemployment was six per cent; 1960, seven per cent; 1961, 7.1 per cent and 1962, 5.9 per cent. I think we are interested in regional figures. The rate of unemployment in 1958 in the Atlantic region was 12.3 per cent. In 1959, it was 10.9 per cent; 1960, 10.5 per cent; 1961, 11.2 per cent and 1962, 10.7 per cent. I put these figures on the record, Mr. Speaker, not as a partisan Liberal, not because I want to engage in this type of debate, but to emphasize the fact that we do not have to go to the hungry thirties to remember unemployment in this country. We only have to go back to the last time the opposition party happened to be in power. When the opposition party was in power, they were faced with problems of an inflation which they inherited. What did they do about it between 1958 and 1962, other than fighting with the Bank of Canada? They ran the unemployment figures in this country to a consistent seven per
cent figure between the years 1958 and 1962, then the Canadian people put them out of office.
I do not want to be dishonest and say that we are not concerned about the December rate of unemployment which was 6.6 per cent. That is not a very nice figure. It does not give me any consolation when I compare it with the 1960 figure. In 1958, today's official opposition had just come into office and their financial policy did not have time to take effect. By 1960, midterm, it had a chance to take effect. The actual figure for unemployment in 1960, and I can give seasonal figures because they are similar, was 8.2 per cent for the month of December. As a matter of fact, the Tories had an interesting year in 1960. In January, 1960 the rate was 8.8 per cent; February, 9.6 per cent; March, 9.7 per cent; April, 8.8 per cent, and right down the line to December when the rate was 8.2 per cent.
But, of course, it is no consolation to the unemployed of today to know that Canadians were in a much more precarious position in 1960. In December, 1962, when the opposition was still in power, the rate of unemployment was 6.3 per cent. It may be interesting to note that when we took over the figure, by years, dropped to 5.1, 4.1, 3.5, 3.6, 4.6, 4.7, 4.7, 6.5. If there is any doubt in anyone's mind as to whether we can lick unemployment, that doubt should be dispelled. We were faced with unemployment when we took power in 1963. We did something about it then, and we are doing something about it now.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Last night I watched the Leader of the Opposition on television. I have also watched other people on television. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will participate in this debate tomorrow. He will show that he made the proper adjustments to his policy as far back as March. He will indicate that we are about the experience an effective stimulation of the economy.
There is one thing missing which would help this country to take off again. The Leader of the Opposition spoke about this as late as February of last year. I am referring to the psychological effect of confidence in this country. If investors, foreign and domestic, who look to Canada as a place to invest their money and stimulate the economy over the next decade, read some of the speeches of gloom and doom which were made this afternoon, they would be damned fools to spend a nickel in this country. Fortunately, they know that the record of Canada is good. They know that we are going to take off again. They know that we are on the right track financially.
We need a bit of confidence, not only from the people of Canada, the bankers and industrialists, but from members opposite. They should understand that the fate of this country depends to a great extent on the future prosperity of the future of this country.
All of us should get together to examine the problem of unemployment. I have not been in the House all that long but, in my view, there is one basic difference between the plight of the unemployed in 1970 as com-

January 18, 1971

pared to 1960. I live in a residential constituency of the island of Montreal. It can be quite adequately described as a workingman's district with railway, Northern Electric and aircraft workers. They suffer unemployment to an unprecedented degree when the economy pulls downward. I remember their plight in 1958, 1959, 1960, 1961 and 1962. Where did they go in 1960? Unemployment insurance benefits were very low in those days as compared even with the present benefits. There was welfare, where welfare existed, but what other programs were on the books to look after the unemployed between 1958 and 1962? There were none, Mr. Speaker. No winter works program, no Department of Manpower, no manpower program. There was no Canada assistance program, no Canada pension plan, no Quebec pension plan. There were no mobility grants, no medicare except in the Province of Saskatchewan and we must pay tribute to hon. gentlemen who belong to the New Democratic Party for that. In fact, there was very little unemployment in Saskatchewan because most of the people were on their way to British Columbia. Statistically, that is so. In any event, there was very little for the unemployed in those days.
The greatest thing we can do for the unemployed is, of course, to provide jobs for them and this should be the prime objective of the present government or of any government. Increasingly, an educated work force demands this, and will continue to do so. But at least we can console ourselves with the knowledge that today the unemployed can turn to some programs. Daily during the question period some people in the opposition laugh at the manpower training program. I do not have to defend the record of that program or of my colleague, the hon. minister responsible for it. However, I looked up the statistics which reflect a program which exists today but which was not in existence during the great depression when the Tories were in power between 1958 and 1962.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has judged me to be intelligent. Coming from him, I consider it to be a real compliment. He is quite a judge.
We spent on manpower training in 1969-70 no less than $245,044,076, a staggering sum of money when we realize it comes out of general revenue. This sum was not placed at the disposal of the unemployed ten years ago. As my colleague mentioned today during the question period, the manpower program not only helps the unemployed by providing a weekly income but it trains unemployed
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
persons to be able to take advantage of the economic upswing when it comes in the next few months.
Since 1960, as a result of prodding by many members of this House-I think it is fair to say they were representative of all parties-we have seen the introduction of the Canada pension plan and the Quebec pension plan. These were not around in the days of 7 per cent and 8 per cent unemployment in 1960. Many regard the Canada pension plan as merely providing a pension at the age of 65 for those who contribute, but those who know the act better realize that it provides an income for people who are prematurely retired from the work force as a result of disability or illness or other circumstances. This program was not around when unemployment reached its highest peak in the sixties but it is one to which the unemployed will be turning increasingly as the plan reaches maturity in the next few years.
There are other programs such as medicare which are of enormous assistance to the unemployed. I have already paid tribute to the NDP for introducing it first in Saskatchewan. It has now been extended across the country and it removes a tremendous financial burden from the shoulders of those least able to pay the cost of hospitalization and medical fees. It is another program which did not exist when the Conservatives were in power and we had a 7 per cent unemployment rate in 1960.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A forward looking minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All kinds of insurance-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Tories came in 1958. Come on!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I did not quote the really bad figures, though I could have done so. I thought 1960 was a good year to quote because hon. gentlemen opposite had had two full years to introduce their economic policies and bring down the unemployment rate. What did they do? Unemployment reached the rate of approximately 7 per cent at a time when there was no manpower program to help the unemployed, no medicare except in one province, no mobility grants to help those who had the necessary skills to move to places where jobs were available. There was no ministry of regional economic expansion capable of directing money to parts of the country which needed it more than others; there was no Canada pension plan, no Quebec pension plan. In short, in 1958 and 1960 there was no alternative but to go on welfare. This is not the case today, because a Liberal government had the foresight and the courage to introduce social legislation between 1963 and 1970 which can now be used for the benefit of those who are temporarily unemployed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Just in case I have been too modest with regard to the accomplishments of this government when describing medicare, we ought not to forget that hospital insurance legislation came in during 1957 or 1958 when the leader of the Liberals in the other place was

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
the Minister of Health and Welfare. I think it was back in 1957. But this action was taken before our government was replaced. As I recall, the opposition party never saw fit to enlarge that program so as to make it even more meaningful, as we have done since 1960.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thank hon. members opposite for their help. They have really been a great help to me.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When will you tell us what you intend to do now?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will tell the House tomorrow-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: God help us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell you what I recommend. Let us not panic or take advantage of this situation in such a way as to make the people feel we are in a depression of the kind we were in between 1958 and 1962. We are not. The Minister of Finance took the proper steps six or eights months ago. They will bear fruit in the early spring, and from then on the number of unemployed will be reduced. The opposition cannot have it both ways. As late as last February, the Leader of the Opposition was talking about the detrimental effect inflation was having, particularly on people living on fixed incomes. One of the statements that he made-this is reported in Hansard though I do not have the page; however, I read everything that the Leader of the Opposition says in debate- was to the effect that we would have to go back a long way to find a country that is in a worse position psychologically than we are today. Having made that statement, what has been the thrust in the debate today of the Leader of the Opposition, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), and even of the leader of the Credi-tistes, who gave us a dissertation on Sweden, the evils of socialism and all the benefits of "funny money"? There has been an almost fiendish glee at the predicament they think the government is in-the high rate of unemployment, gloom and doom.
Since the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) reduced the interest rate and freed the money supply in this country, there has been ample money in the banks of this country for investment, borrowing and economic expansion. But we must get over the psychological hurdle first. If I were a businessman sitting in the Gallery today listening to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and of other speakers, I would ask what kind of country this is. I would say to myself: "If they have no more confidence in our future than that displayed by their speeches, why should I invest my money in such a country?" I think all of us, the opposition as well as the government, have a responsibility to create the right psychological climate for investors to invest. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out in February, psychology is a very important weapon in the fight against unemployment and the lack of investment.
I have been sitting here since two-thirty listening to speeches in the hope that someone would bring forward a blueprint. But when I heard the Leader of the Opposition repeating some editorials, then I knew there was nothing new in his approach. He talked of reducing income tax in the hope that some money would find its way into the economy sooner or later.
The hon. member for York South made it very clear today that he would reduce taxes, but only personal income tax not corporation tax. Somehow this would stimulate the economy, and so he wants it all ways. I presume the hon. gentleman must have been hampered by the shortness of time in his interview last night, because today I expected him to expand on the kind of programs he would introduce if he were head of the government. He said that perhaps he would take off the building tax since our housing starts are not going to break any records with or without the tax. Certainly, the sales on building materials in no way has impeded our housing starts for this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are 20 per cent short this year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not because of this tax. We are now reaching our target because we have injected into the economy the money necessary for the construction of the low cost housing which the people need. Built in the right part of the country, this housing will do a lot to reduce inflation and to create a surplus of housing in those areas.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know what it is about my mannerisms that so upsets the opposition members today, though they seem to make more sense sitting down than when they stand up to make speeches. However, this is not unusual for hon. members on the other side. If hon. members think I have not much to say, then I am continuing this debate as it began two hours ago. What has disappointed me in this debate is that there has not been one fresh idea put forward by any member of the opposition as to how he would tackle the problem of unemployment. That is, of course, apart from the representative from the Creditiste party.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A question of privilege, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Peace River is rising on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before this debate commenced I rose and suggested that if the government would see fit, through the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Sharp), to bring in supplementary estimates-and I indicated at least four specific items-we would be prepared to suggest that the debate be abandoned. I have not spoken in the debate; I simply raised a point of order to make that suggestion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said "new suggestions", and the hon. member has not made a new suggestion in the last ten years. His only answer is that we spend more
[Mr. Mackasey.)
January 18, 1971

money, though he does not tell us how we should spend it. He is a member of the party which a couple of years ago complained about the size of the deficit of this government and the effect that it was having on pushing up interest rates in Canada. Interest rates were being driven upwards and therefore this affected investment and borrowing. Hon. gentlemen opposite now want it both ways. As I say, they are barren of new ideas. I was referring to new, refreshing ideas.
Once again the Minister of Finance will emphasize, as he patiently did a few weeks ago, the steps that he has taken during the last six months to stimulate the economy of this country. He will review the funds that he has placed at the disposal of the provinces amounting to $150 million. He will remind hon. members of the drastic decrease in interest rates that has been characteristic of our banking system during the last few months. He will remind hon. members of the injection of money into the housing field. He will mention the $50 million put at the disposal of the unemployed this winter.
Hon. members have talked about extending benefits to the unemployed during winter. Surely, they should know that even under the present scheme benefits are extended on a seasonal basis during the winter. The requirement for eligibility for unemployment insurance benefits in this country are relaxed in order to extend the period of coverage. Virtually any member of the work force is eligible for seasonal benefits if he is laid off during the winter months. So, this is not new; it is already in operation.
It has also been suggested that we should introduce some new programs. The hon. member for York South suggested the immediate payment of $100 a week to people in receipt of unemployment inusrance benefits. I know what the hon. member meant; he meant to a maximum of $100 a week-I do not think the leader of the Creditistes made that clear-or two-thirds of salary up to a maximum of $100 a week take home pay. The unemployment insurance commission plan is designed to do more than simply turn over money to the unemployed. It is designed to co-ordinate the efforts of the departments of manpower, health and welfare, labour, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and other social agencies across the country that have a common interest in the work force of this country.
I would be insulting the members of this House if I suggested that unemployment could be solved immediately; that we can continue to compete with other countries that are highly automated. To do this we must first rationalize the textile industry in Quebec, for one, which is so labour-intensive that it will price itself out of existence if it does not automate. Automation may, of course, cause some unemployment, at least temporary unemployment, until this new automated industry becomes competitive with that of other countries.
This is a process now going on in the textile industry, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) mentioned some months ago. The minister may or may not have mentioned that he is also studying the shoe industry. Where Canadian industry is fully automated
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
and has the economy of scale that the auto and steel industries have, then Canadian workers are as productive, in some cases more productive, than their United States or Swedish counterparts. But this requires new thinking on the part of governments. It means, at times, having the courage to create temporary unemployment intentionally.
It takes a great degree of courage for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to say to the textile industry of Quebec: "If you want to survive you must rationalize your industry. You must accept automation and technological change. You must let us help you rationalize your industry, even if this puts 50 per cent of the workers in the textile industry out of work temporarily". Because this kind of automation is the key solution to our problem. We must make the transition from labour-intensive industry to highly automated industry or this country will not survive in the export market. Certainly, we cannot survive simply by exporting primary products. Our production must be competitive and we must expand our exports of secondary products. This will result when we automate labour-intensive industries such as textiles and shoes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where are the new ideas?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They are newer than the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but I do so to advise him and the chamber that his time has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Continue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent that the hon. member continue?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, I cannot satisfy everybody at once.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Talk about the seventies.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I rarely can understand what anyone says when he talks in his sleep. If the hon. member wants to talk in his sleep, he should go outside. It takes courage sometimes to create unemployment. We have created unemployment in the textile industry and we will probably create it temporarily in other industries as we automate and as we rationalize these industries.
So far as the Unemployment Insurance Act is concerned, it should be before the House fairly soon. The co-operation of the particular committee which was seized of this problem, and which met during the summer months and early fall, was commendable. I gather its report was fairly unanimous. If my review of the recommendations is accurate, the report endorses most of the proposals in the white paper. July 1 is the
2508

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Mackasey
target date in respect of the legislation and with the usual co-operation of the House I visualize little difficulty in meeting that target date. The new plan will, I believe, provide not only more moneys for the temporarily unemployed of this country, but will provide a better education for people where education is a problem or is the root cause of unemployment. This should help young people as they enter the work force for the first time. Several members, quite properly, alluded to these people. The government will have to look after the older people who are affected by automation. This will be done through other plans such as the TAB program which was introduced simultaneously with the auto pact. When we rationalize the auto industry it will be up to the government to do something for the people who are displaced because of age or because of an inability to adjust to the new plan so that they will be able to finish their days with dignity.
In conclusion, let me say I take no consolation in the high rate of unemployment, but I am consoled by the fact that although the number of unemployed people in 1970 has been relatively high it has been much lower than in the period between 1958 and 1962 when the Tories were in power. The people now are better off because they have at their disposal not only manpower programs, the Canada pension plan, the Quebec pension plan, transitional benefits, mobility grants, but also additional jobs because of regional and economic expansion. Together with others, these are programs designed to help the Canadian people as a right and not as a privilege.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) is rising to ask a question, but since the minister's time has expired it would have to be asked with unanimous consent of the House. Is there such unanimous consent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would merely ask the minister, since he referred to the manpower training plan, whether he retained in his mind the fact that those who are in receipt of allowances and are receiving training are not included in the figure of 538,000 unemployed. If they were considered as unemployed, another 100,000 would have to be added to that figure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has made my point. The 1960 figure would be 100,000 higher because there was no manpower program in those days. In setting up the proper department, we had the vision to provide the proper measures to take 100,000 people off the unemployment rolls and give them up to $108 a week under certain circumstances as well as provide them with an adequate upgrading of their skills and their education where necessary.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member rising to ask a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Would the minister also agree that, in addition to having high unemployment
in Canada, in 1971 we have the highest cost of living this country has had for a great period of time?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, the Leader of the Opposition today mentioned the very tools we used to combat inflation. He suggested that one thing we must not do is lose track of the need to continue voluntary restraints in wages and prices. I think these were his words. In other words, he endorsed precisely the policies introduced by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Order, before I see the hon.
member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin), perhaps hon. members would permit me to deal with the notice required in respect of the adjournment proceedings this evening.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the speech that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) just delivered.
Even with my great admiration for the minister, I must say that his speech is the weakest he ever made since he became Minister of Labour and that it merely amounts to an attempt to justify the government's incompetence in dealing with unemployment.
When a Minister of Labour feels the need to uphold the government's position, to refer to the previous

January 18, 1971

administration, namely the Progressive Conservative administration, and to compare unemployment figures for 1958, 1960, 1962 with the present statistics, this shows that the government is unable to come up with a solution to solve the present unemployment problem.
The minister says: We, in the government, need the understanding of the population and of the members; we seek their suggestions to solve the unemployment problem. I could retort to the minister and to the government members that we have been making suggestions for a year and a half. However, every time the opposition has made representations or suggestions and a problem was settled, the government hastened to say. The opposition had nothing to do with that, we on the government side found the solution.
In this house we have often said and I say it again: the government was elected to administer the country. It is not up to the opposition, but rather to the government, to solve the problems now facing the Canadian people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we analyze the speech delivered by the Minister of Labour, we find that the government offers no solution but acts as if it did not care a hang about the problem and the required solutions.
The opposition has been talking about unemployment We can recall that from 1958 to 1963 when we were in power, the former prime minister or the former hon. member for Essex-East used to ask questions to the government about the unemployment situation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: But there was no unemployment at that time!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There was and it may have been the reason behind our defeat in 1963. It also explains why this government will be defeated in 1972 unless they find solutions to cope with this national problem.
Some hon Members: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But recalling the past will not solve our problem. We must look ahead and the government should be able to tell us the kind of solutions they are considering.
In September 1970, the Economic Council of Canada warned the government about the unemployment situation, as we can see on page 21 of the report titled:
"Performance and Potential mid-1950's to mid-1970's", and I quote:
We regard recent and current rates of unemployment as unacceptably high. Canada probably now has the highest rate of unemployment among the more industrially advanced nations, even after allowance for the differences in the bases for unemployment estimates. The current rate is about double the medium-term target for Canada suggested in our Sixth Annual Review. The building up of unemployment to such high levels reflects a very considerable enlargement of burdens and hardships imposed on individuals and families. It also reflects a considerable waste of human resources and a large economic cost to the whole society.
23786-18i
The Budget-Mr. Asselin
All that can be found in that report.
Reducing this high level of unemployment must therefore be considered-in human, social and economic terms-as a matter of the highest priority.
What is the present situation? As a Quebec member I would like tonight to describe the present situation in Quebec.
At the time of the last provincial election, the Quebec people were given false hopes. Seconded by the federal Liberal party, Mr. Bourassa stated that in 1971 he would create 100,000 jobs. This was a fine electoral slogan. The unemployed who heard that promise could think that among those 100,000 jobs there would surely be one for him. The Liberal party got into office in Quebec thanks to it.
It was said that if the Liberal party was elected in Quebec while a Liberal government was in power in Ottawa, there would no longer be any problems for Que-bekers. Everything would be fine. What is the present situation in Quebec? We have there 197,000 unemployed, i.e. 8.4 per cent of the working population as compared to 7.2 per cent in November and 6.7 per cent for the same period in 1969.
In Quebec, the number of unemployed has increased by
31.000	in one month only and this is exactly half the unemployment increase for the whole of Canada.
The City of Montreal has 2,000 more unemployed than last year at the same date. There were 62,346 unemployed at the end of December. In 1970, only 10,000 jobs have been created in Quebec as compared to 50,000 the preceding year. And the Union Nationale government of that time was no good. It has created 50,000 new jobs in 1969. It is reasonable to hope that this total will reach
14.000	when December figures will be known. In the first eleven months of 1970, there were 10,000 new jobs and
23.000	new unemployed due to the fact that there were
33.000	more people in the labour force.
Such a statement of affairs makes responsible people think because it is a dark picture and it brings people close to desperation. In short, this situation is intolerable in a country such as ours.
We are talking about 25,000 young jobless in Montreal. Many of them are educated.
One of the most modern education systems has been introduced in Quebec. I agree on that point. But the present government forgot one other principle: when providing retraining and trying to educate the young people, we must also find employment opportunities for them. This has not been anticipated!
This is why when we are in our office or in our constituency, people come to ask for employment. They are almost desperate when they realize that conditions are worsening from day to day with no prospective solution to their problems.
Without making any practical suggestion, the Minister of Labour merely blames the previous administration even though the unemployment rate is higher at the present time.

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Asselin
It is not surprising then to note that there is turmoil and dissent in Quebec. It is not surprising that the Quebec Minister of Labour, Mr. Cournoyer, stated not long ago: If conditions do not improve, the number of persons bent on revolution will increase! If we do not take all possible steps if we do not face the conditions and reality, what worries me is that we will never have enough policemen to control the reactions of those victims of our system.
He is not the only one to say such things. The Quebec premier, Mr. Bourassa, said last week that he was concerned and questioned the possibility of creating 100,000 jobs. He did not propose any solution, neither did he say what measures his government might adopt in order to remedy the situation.
Also in the province of Quebec, leaders in industry are sounding the alarm. Mr. Daoust, for instance, said that a disaster is imminent when one finds an 8.4 percent rate of unemployment in Quebec, and that 11,500 permanent jobs were lost last year.
Last night, I read in the papers that such an important concern as SOGEFOR was laying off 800 workers. This concern is made up of four plants which have cost the public and private sectors $9 million.
When we know that 52.8 per cent of business bankruptcies reported in Canada take place in Quebec and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) feels satisfied with the steps taken by his government until now to correct the situation, I say that the government shirks its responsibilities.
Mr. Speaker, what are the causes of such a situation? Obviously some will say it is the October crisis, but the October crisis did not come out of the blue. On the contrary, it had roots; unrest existed before but the government had not been wise to it.
The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was saying this afternoon that the main cause of this unrest was the fiscal policy of this government. In this regard, I would like to have recorded in Hansard a statement made by Claude Ryan of the newspaper he Devoir, in the January 18 1971 issue, in connection with the fiscal policy of the government, which reads as follows:
With regard to public finance, the Trudeau government has followed one of the most reactionary policies . .. Obsessed with the idea of a balanced budget, it has forced provincial and municipal governments, by driving them to deficit budgeting through its fiscal miserliness, to increase their debt abroad-
The government has also-
-withdrawn from the private sector such a large share of the national product that this sector has lost much of its punch-
-at the expense of the majority of workers. Thus-
-numerous categories of citizens, who depend more directly on government allowances, have been reduced to an income level close to poverty.
Mr. Speaker, if our country is to survive, the time has come to return to a more dynamic concept of public finance. I continue to quote:
The government should offer new incentives to economic agents whose decisions and creativity are essential to economic development.
For almost three months we have been asking the government to re-establish the winter works program so that instead of making people dependent on welfare funds or unemployment insurance as the present government wants to do, paying them measly allowances, they may be provided with jobs.
Many of our welfare recipients are not interested in welfare grants. A large number of them are on welfare because they have to be. Most of them would like to have jobs.
Why did not the government re-activate the winter works program? It will be said that the system produced fraud. This is obvious. But it is possible to pass legislation to prevent it. It is more interesting for a person who is engaged in winter works, in a municipality, to earn $15 a day than to receive a scanty allowance of $150 a month. He is less inclined to idleness and passivity.
Mr. Speaker, we made suggestions to the government. When we asked it to remove the 11 per cent tax on building materials, why did it turn a deaf ear? It would have been possible thus to provide work for the unemployed. People would have sold more manufactured products.
When the government was requested to drop the 3 per cent surtax, what did the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) answer? It had been imposed for one year only. The Minister of Finance maintained it.
I heard this afternoon the leader of the Ralliement creditiste (Mr. Caouette) speak about taxes, the 3 per cent surtax; it is his party that voted in favour of maintaining the 3 per cent surtax in 1967-along with the government.
Mr. Speaker, when when will the federal government give up part of its jurisdiction to the provinces so as to permit them to use the best economic means to face their situation?
This afternoon I put a question to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (M. Marchand) who answered that the federal government had given Quebec $150 million to fight unemployment. Then we are told that from those $150 million, $68 million will be earmarked for the building of roads in Montreal. How many jobs will this create, Mr. Speaker? Fourteen hundred jobs for $68 million! The building of roads entails expropriations, the purchase of land; judiciary and extrajudiciary expenses have to be paid. Then, is it logical to grant $68 million to fight unemployment and create only 1,400 jobs in Quebec? I am not blaming the Quebec government for accepting this money and for building roads in Montreal but I suggest that it is illogical that only 1,400 jobs should follow.
I am taking the floor because I represent a riding where unemployment is at its peak and 25 per cent of

January 18, 1971

the labour force is idle. When the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion claims that the granting of subsidies is creating employment I say that they are not distributed proportionately throughout the province, since several ridings of the Lower St. Lawrence region and the North Shore have received nothing.
We have made representations. At Sacre-Cceur, in my riding, a card-board plant has been set up by the C.F.U. and the farmers have invested several thousands of dollars into it. Government help is necessary and we need a few million dollars. We called on the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. We were sent back to Quebec to inquire whether the Quebec government would agree to the proposal. Mr. Speaker, this cardboard plant at Sacre-Cceur could provide jobs for some 1,500 people.
To what use were put the grants from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion? Indeed, such grants have helped some industries, but have jobs been created in numbers as large as was hoped? Have the unemployed benefited from them to the maximum? It was said today that automation and technology have entered the labour market. Formulas should be found to directly help a worker find employment. And this is the challenge that this Parliament and especially this government should meet considering the tragic situation facing us at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, there is also need for a more thorough selection for retraining among the labour force. In that respect, huge amounts of money are being lost in my own constituency and in several others in the province.
In my constituency, housewives are attending seventh grade classes, to receive $60 per week of course. The housewife hires a babysitter for $15 per week, and she earns $60 per week while retraining. For what purpose does she need retraining?
Retraining courses should be more rigorously selective, to prevent the taxpayers' money from being wasted in such a shocking way.
Mr. Speaker, the government's employment policy and fight against unemployment have failed. They resorted right off to a long term policy. What is being done? Were there consultations with the economic councils and Chambers of Commerce of each area? Those people, Mr. Speaker, have studied all aspects of the situation. They spend hours and hours examining economic conditions in their area and find solutions to their problems. The Minister of Economic Regional Expansion as well as the Department of Labour should immediately have a mobile team meet the responsible persons from those regional economic councils as well as the Chambers of Commerce to seek advice from them on projects that could be launched immediately in order to alleviate unemployment in Canada and especially in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, another way would be to ask this government whether they are really willing to fight unemployment. A federal-provincial conference on unemployment problems should be convened immediately, a conference
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
which municipalities' representatives could attend so as to find solutions to this acute problem. When an emergency occurred in Quebec, emergency measures were passed. Unemployment has now become an urgent issue and the government should take the steps available to them to cope with the situation.
Should the government, in spite of all our suggestions, Mr. Speaker, persist in not making rapid, urgent and efficient decisions in order to fight against unemployment, it will show that this government was not sincere when they talked about war on poverty, that the prime minister's "just society" slogan was merely window-dressing and that the government was not ready for action. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I say that if the necessary steps are not taken in order to cope with this problem, this government will be very severely judged by the Canadian people on the day of reckoning.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an understatement to say that the time has come for us to shift primary emphasis in economic strategy for policies of restraint to expansionist policies. In the budget address, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) was pleased to note how well Canada has succeeded in containing inflation. Perhaps we have succeeded too well.
Since we are a relatively thin economy which is dependent upon foreign trade more than any other country in the world, we cannot afford to have a rate of inflation which exceeds that of our trading partners, making our goods uncompetitive. On the other hand, it is not good for us to have zero inflation when inflation gallops ahead in countries which are our suppliers and our customers. If we have zero inflation, or an acceleration too far below that of the rest, we find, especially with the long-term capital inflows which Canada generally attracts, the balance of payments pressures pushing our dollar upward. Thus there is the possibility of as much damage in this direction being caused as accelerating prices would cause. The hardness of our dollar, in which the minister took such pride, can be as much a problem as inflation itself. This, for example, is the testimony of the pulp and paper industries.
The target, I suggest, is to have only slightly better performance than the others. It is easy enough to say this, but the implication is that our policy has to be that of hitting a moving target whose momentum can only be guessed, and of having to fire the shots well ahead of time. This, I feel, shows how tough the job of formulating price stability policies can be. No one has to be reminded that fiscal and monetary price stability policies which have been pursued have implications on economic growth and employment and that in some areas the results produced by the government's policies have been unacceptable, especially if one considers the regional implications.
It is too simple and too misleading to focus on one economic performance target at a time. When ministers of finance assess the performance of the economy and make their periodic prescriptions, they must do so in terms of a number of goals and not just shoot at one.

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Kaplan
These important goals include full employment, reasonable price stability, sustained economic growth and a stable balance of payments.
Looking at the problem around us in the Canadian economy today we can see how difficult it can be for the government to meet the challenge of finding that balance. Why is it so hard? The measure of the challenge has a number of dimensions. They are: First, the apparent cyclical nature of a free market economy. Second, the extent of our dependence upon foreign influences over which Canada has no control, both in the international market for capital, long and short term, and in the international market for commodities and goods. Third, the division of jurisdiction over the public sector in our federal system, with its implications for taxing, borrowing and spending. Fourth, the lag between the occurrence of economic events and the collection of sufficient information to permit them to be seen. Fifth, the lag between the taking of corrective action and the coming into effect of such action. A final element is the limited number of measures which the government has chosen so far to adopt in order to achieve the economic performance goals. This is the aspect of the problem on which I wish to concentrate.
The present administration has increased the number of measures that it is prepared to adopt, but not far enough. Fiscal and monetary policies have been relied on, and their regional and sectoral impacts have been sharpened by this government more than by any of its predecessors. In addition, more effective measures to increase the geographical and occupational mobility of labour have been devised and heavily financed. Rationalization of industries, agricultural, industrial and financial, is taking place to some degree, with important government intervention. Hopefully, more will take place through an improved competition policy which has been promised for this month. There are efforts to improve the workings of the marketplace through better consumer information.
The budget that we are debating, Mr. Speaker, calls for a direct stimulation to the economy. The Minister of Finance has referred to it as a $2 billion shift in direction. Some critics would like to see the government spending more, and spending it faster. In addition, there are calls for sweeping tax relief. I ask, what are the implications of this about-face which is indicated in economic policy? After buying price stability by paying so high a social cost in unemployment-a toll which may get worse before it gets better-is the government going to abandon the inflation battle without taking precautions against the recurrence of inflation? The hard fact is that for all the experience of the last 18 months we are launching the economy into a phase in which there will inevitably be increased pressure on prices, which will heat up the economy, and yet we have produced no new tools for cooling it off. The government's defence to this charge is that the expansionary policies chosen are more selective than expansionist policies have been in the past. I submit that these assurances are not entirely convincing.
Canada, Mr. Speaker, needs a policy of selective controls on prices and incomes. We need machinery to con-

trol prices, to control rents, to control wages and to control incomes. Jawboning does not work, public pressure does not work, guidelines do not work, and voluntary formulas have failed for want of volunteers. We need a system of controls, and so far this government, which has been very determined in its economic policies, has not had the guts to propose one. Especially in dealing with the labour sector, the government has not yet shown the kind of courage which will achieve results. Of course, a system of controls presents its own problems.
Firstly, it should be recognized that a free market is preferable to one with controls. The Gallup polls recently taken tell us that the public is prepared to accept price controls. But how much public understanding is there of the implications? One of the fundamental values in our society is the free bargaining process, labour being free to bargain for the price it is to be paid for its services and producers being free to determine the goods which they wish to produce and the prices they will seek to obtain. Whatever policy of controls we adopt, its ultimate objective should be a return to the free market. Second, selective controls are inevitably unfair because they permit the sectors which are not selected to continue to exercise whatever market pressure they can, and in the state of our present marketplace this can be considerable. For this reason, a package of controls would have to be selected on a basis which would be politically acceptable to a broad cross-section of the Canadian people.
It seems clear that the danger area in the economy today is wage pressure. This is demonstrated by the price performance of labour in the market in the past year of economic decline. Historically, the labour market has responded like other markets to pressures of supply and demand. More recently, labour, especially unionized labour, has ceased to be a dependent variable in the economic picture. Wage increases are an inexorable, independent variable: they tend to move independently, irrespective of market forces.
In contrast by no stretch of the imagination can corporate profits, however measured, be considered the culprit in today's inflation. Notwithstanding this, I cannot imagine an imposed control on labour costs being acceptable or successful without some control on rent, which is one of the greatest and fastest growing expenses of the average Canadian. Again, justice would require some control over the incomes of the professionals who serve the public and of management personnel, particularly in the key industries which might be chosen for wage control. A third consideration is that the controls must be used on a short-term basis.
It can be seen that permanent price and incomes controls could not be selective. They would have to be comprehensive, otherwise there would be a damaging distortion of the economy as resources moved from the controlled to the uncontrolled sectors. Further, the longer the term of the control period, the more complex the machinery would have to be. Inevitable inequities, which may be sustainable on a short-term basis, would have to
January 18, 1971

be ironed out by reviews and appeals as the term lengthened.
A final problem that I want to touch on is the need that such machinery be established and put into place quickly when it is required, complete with the bureaucracy needed for administration and policing, and the necessity of communicating quickly to all individuals affected a clear understanding of their responsibilities. For this reason, I would propose that Parliament enact a kind of economic war measures act, that is to say, that a control system be legislated but not put into effect for the time being.
Let us have a proposal from the government that can be considered by Parliament, interested groups and the public at large. Let us improve it as a system through the process of public participation; and then let it sit on the shelf for implementation if and when special sectors or regions of the economy begin to heat up as expansionary policies now being debated take effect. Then when the powers are required to be put into place, there will be the public understanding and acceptance which is necessary to make them work, and there will be an effective method of breaking the spine of the inflationary spiral.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget speech shows vividly that the government and its advisers do not realize what is going on in the economy of this country. In view of the unemployment figures recently released, the budget speech, which when presented was an admission of the uncertainty of the government on the unlikely course of economic developments in Canada, has now shown further the grossly inadequate appreciation that this government has of the economic situation.
The budget, Mr. Speaker, is the product of a man who really does not know where the ball is going to bounce. It offered no immediate stimulus to the economy. It was based on an assumption that the economy will swing up. In the most recent unemployment figures, as has been reviewed by my colleagues, we have seen the numbers of persons unemployed leap to the highest point experienced in Canada in ten years. What was the reaction of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to this situation? It was the usual verbal platitude, "that new measures included in the budget... would start to take effect in the near future". I would like to know what the Minister of Finance means when he uses the word "start". When does he intend to start? It is obvious that he has not started yet? How does he intend to start? There is certainly nothing in this minibudget to allow for even a ministart-and what is required is very much more. It would seem obvious, Mr. Speaker, that this government has only one economic transmission, start, stop and reverse, but obviously no ahead.
At the end of last December there were in Canada
150,000	more people unemployed than at the same time a year ago. In total, 538,000 able-bodied Canadians were unable to find work. This figure of 538,000, Mr. Speaker, is the number of people eligible for work, but a great many others are affected and affected directly by these
The Budget-Mr. Moores
people not being able to find employment. Taking the average number of dependants per worker in Canada, we have between 1,700,000 and 1,800,000 Canadians, men, women and children, directly suffering the cruel effects of unemployment. This means that the number of people directly affected by unemployment in Canada today is more than the population of any province in Canada with the exception of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia. In fact, it is more than the total population of the three Maritime provinces.
The present situation has been reached as a direct result of government action in certain areas, and inaction in others. At no time have we seen planning with wisdom, or even reaction, once the crisis was obvious. Even now, when the crisis is upon us, what is the government's position? The Acting Prime Minister noted that the government had predicted a steady reduction in unemployment and now says, "We have no reason to change this forecast". He further indicated that the government has no immediate plans or new crash programs aimed at easing unemployment.
I think it is now quite obvious to even the most complacent Canadians-except the government, which seems to be the most complacent of all-that this government is incapable not only of planning with any degree of wisdom but of even carrying out any worth while plan that may be offered by others. We have a situation facing Canada that approaches the catastrophic, and it is handled by the Acting Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the other ministers with all the initiative we have come to expect from computerized inertia. Successful programs and accurate forecasting have never been the government's strong point, yet members of the cabinet are quoted as remaining optimistic about the economy and are sticking by earlier forecasts predicting a steady reduction in unemployment. This afternoon we heard the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) say it took courage to create unemployment. He seemed to be proud of it. I say it will take wisdom to correct it, and this is what is lacking.
We have been advised that the ranks of the unemployed have risen by 13 per cent since the end of November-40 per cent above the figure at this time last year. And still the government remains optimistic. What does it take to persuade the government to accept the reality that a very real crisis faces the country and that something must be done about it? We need a great deal more than we have witnessed lately, which one could almost call government by extrasensory perception.
One of the characteristics of the government since its election is that it has treated people as if they were numbers: it has depended upon the computer to provide the answers, when what is needed is realization that Canadians are individuals, individuals with human emotions. People cannot be computerized, nor can their emotions. By failing to recognize this, the government has been responsible for the cruelest neglect and waste of the greatest resource a country can have-the people themselves. The government deliberately ran down the econo-

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Moores
my in order, we are told, to fight inflation. What we have seen is the fighting of inflation at any cost-and the cost has been far too great. The unhappy feature all along is that the government has been behind the play; it was late getting on to inflation, and late getting off. It took so long to recognize the situation that it had to go for the overkill.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was quoted as saying on December 23 that inflation had been licked. Inflation may have been temporarily subdued, Mr. Speaker, but for the Prime Minister of Canada to encourage the public to believe that inflation has been licked is misleading. Wage increases during the last six months cannot but be reflected in price increases in 1971. The bond market, which is the best indication of the government's handling of the economy, exposes the Prime Minister's statement that inflation has been licked. Rates for long-term lending are still very high, and the long-term security yield has budged almost not at all.
The treasurer of the Ontario government, Mr. Mac-Naughton, called upon the federal government on December 7 to expand the output of the economy, to stimulate the economies of high-growth regions. He warned provincial and municipal governments that they would be forced into incurring higher levels of borrowing and/or tax increases if Ottawa continued its policy conducive to low average growth. One step the Minister of Finance should have taken immediately was the ending of the 3 per cent surtax. Canadians expected him to announce tax cuts to stimulate the economy. Instead, he imposed an additional tax, as it were, by retaining the surtax.
Canada cannot afford continued excessive unemployment. The Economic Council estimates the country has lost $3 billion in production because of high unemployment levels. The government accepts this inhumane, disgraceful fact with complacency. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) was quoted on January 2 as saying he would accept an unemployment rate of 6 per cent, or even a rate as high as 10 per cent. No Canadian should accept this, Mr. Speaker, and any representative of the Canadian electors who does should resign.
The supplementary estimates approved in the closing hours before the Christmas recess are another indication of the direction of economic policies of this government. Sixty-nine million extra dollars were needed to finance the public debt because the government had been forced to borrow more than was originally intended. Fifty-one million extra dollars were needed for payment to the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan because more people were on dole, had been forced on dole, than was expected.
What the government does not realize, apparently, is that once the economy has intentionally been slowed down, it cannot be stimulated again by words alone. People who a few years ago were expanding and developing the economy as entrepreneurs have become frightened of government policies and are reluctant to begin again where they left off. You cannot just turn a switch and change the mood of the people. Something much more positive and meaningful must be done to get
the economy going again. A great many businesses have slowed to a walk. The easing of interest rates on money probably means they will not actually go bankrupt, but neither will they develop to the extent which is required. Speaking of bankruptcy, I say that mental bankruptcy seems to be the forte of this government. It is vital that hon. gentlemen opposite admit they are wrong, if only for the sake of the people they were elected to serve.
The stark statistics of unemployment are the most eloquent comment which can be made on the failure of the government's economic policies. The Minister of Finance cannot, or will not, offer the slightest hope that the worst may be over. Neither can he fall back upon some statistical rationalization by saying that the seasonally adjusted rate is improving. It rose last month, and there is every indication that later this winter these figures will become much worse. Yet the government carries on in the same optimistic vein, predicting that things will get better soon.
Regardless of what the government may say, unemployment is the direct result of its economic mismanagement. Surely members opposite must realize by now that their policies are altogether inadequate. I plead with the Minister of Finance to be honest and truthful with the people. We must tell the people the truth about the seriousness of unemployment, and the government should release its forecasts showing how bad it is likely to get. Only after first admitting the gravity of the situation will we be able to find a solution for it.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At six o'clock the House took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying at six o'clock, before the government can find a solution to unemployment it must appreciate the enormity of the problem facing Canada. Trying to curtail inflation by creating unemployment has not worked in other countries and it will not work in Canada. The government's policy of deliberately creating massive unemployment to stem inflation is wrong. It is easy for me to criticize lack of action by this government over the past year or so, but the future is what is important now. Where do we, as a nation, go from here? What can we do to initiate a policy that will not only correct the present situation but ensure that a similiar situation does not happen again in the years ahead?
It is essential that we implement tax cuts, as was outlined by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) today, and it is imperative that the Minister of Finance give consideration to making these tax cuts immediately for the good of this country. Even doing this now will

January 18, 1971

mean that it will take time before the effect is fully felt, but it is imperative that it be done now in order that the situation does not get out of hand. The over-all Canadian economy must be put back on the track, and it is the duty of this government to take the first step by acting now.
High unemployment affects all Canada, but particularly the have-not regions. In my province of Newfoundland the situation is very much worse than in any other province in Canada. At the end of last August, the provincial department of social services and rehabilitation revealed that 93,000 Newfoundlanders were receiving assistance from that department. That in itself indicates that almost 19 per cent of the population are on social assistance. The recent unemployment figures show that
68.000	men, women and children in Newfoundland are directly affected by unemployment. This, in a province with just 500,000 total population, is a staggering statistic.
One notices in the statistics for all of Canada that
8.940.000	was the number of people in the work force in November, 1970, and 8,329,000 was the work force in December. This is a drop of 611,000 people in the work force in one month. The minister shakes his head, but these are the figures published by the department. These
611.000	people find it impossible to get work, and after many calls to manpower have just given up in frustration. Many of this group live in areas such as Newfoundland where work opportunities just do not exist. Their dropping out of the work force is now shown in the unemployment figures. I believe that if an accurate assessment were made of the Newfoundland work force, it would show close to 20 per cent of our population presently unemployed, and this figure will increase as the winter progresses.
The Premier of Newfoundland does not even admit that we have an unemployment problem. As a matter of fact, a short time ago one of his ministers said on a television program that a "wave of prosperity" was sweeping across the province. No problem will ever be solved if those in authority do not first realize that it exists. In Newfoundland the government is forecasting a miniboom for next summer. If this occurs, so much the better. But the question should be asked: What about next winter? What we are seeing in Newfoundland is the creation of temporary jobs of a seasonal nature, with virtually no consideration being given to long-term prospects. The Premier is introducing a master plan-or, as some prefer to call it, "The master's plan"-at an economic conference he has called for February 4, 5 and 6.
Any plan for Newfoundland would have to include heavy inputs of money from the federal government. Yet last Monday in this House, when asked if any special plan was being prepared for Newfoundland, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) admitted having no knowledge of such a plan and afterwards intimated that he did not have any knowledge of the
The Budget-Mr. Moores
conference. This is the type of harebrain scheme we have come to expect from the provincial government in Newfoundland. There are promises and more promises, but very little is accomplished.
Newfoundland is badly in need of a plan for its future development. It needs a great deal more than the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has provided to date. An infrastructure for industrial development is being established. No one can say that services are not required nor that they are not desirable, but they will be meaningful only if the people who are to use them have the opportunity to earn enough to maintain a decent standard of living, which is not the case at present.
A short while ago the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council met with the House committee here in Ottawa. They suggested that Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland be included in the incentives program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which is to be made available for primary industries. I agree with this and believe it is very essential. The federal government, with approval of the provincial government, has a wrong order of priorities. The problems of Newfoundland are very different from those of Montreal. The type of urban, bureaucratic thinking we have had to date will not work in Newfoundland.
The Atlantic Advisory Council was commissioned to undertake a study in Newfoundland to determine why the regional incentives program is not working. It is not working, and the minister and his department are aware of this. I hope when they find the answer they will come up with something that will be workable in our province. To date the program of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has created very few permanent jobs in Newfoundland. The reason is that the department responsible for that program has ignored the resource development of our province which many people, including myself, feel is by far the top priority if we in Newfoundland are to establish our identity. Our people must develop an excellence in what they know, and they must develop the industries that are natural to their situation. It is not reasonable to expect Newfoundland to develop a sophisticated industrialized base. The people of Newfoundland have not been trained for sophisticated industry. Our people have a knowledge of the industries with which they are familiar. The people of Newfoundland want the industries to become better than they already are.
The future of rural Newfoundland must include the development of the resource industries and the establishment of an excellence in respect of these industries. It makes no more sense to establish an industrialized base in Newfoundland whereby our people would have to become involved in scientific training, than it does to ask the maitre d' of the Queen Elizabeth Hotel to operate a chainsaw. We must develop our primary industries, which would include direct assistance to small operations based on raw materials such as fish, lumber, minerals, agricultural products, and so on. We are witnessing a program that will create part-time jobs while what we must have is full-time employment.
January 18, 1971

The Budget-Mr. Osier
Our people must be given the opportunity to contribute to this great nation. Regardless of the Premier's attitude there is in Newfoundland a reawakening of the people who want to opt in. Our people in Newfoundland are basically peaceful, but they are becoming fed up with government mismanagement and misinterpretation both at the federal and provincial levels. They want opportunities. They want to play their part in Canada and not be treated as second-class citizens. It is the responsibility of the federal government to develop programs that will realistically help develop provinces such as Newfoundland. It must be realized that the people in these areas will never have the same degree of affluence we find in large Canadian cities. However, the degree of affluence must be increased so that the people can live decently and enjoy the many advantages their locations provide.
The province of Newfoundland has a great future. The resource potential is greater than that of the other Atlantic provinces put together. This resource potential must be exploited for the benefit of all the people and not just a few, as is presently the case. As I said earlier, the people of Canada cannot be treated as just so many numbers. Each individual and each region is different, and all in their own way have a contribution to make. This has not been appreciated by the present government, and it must be if our country is to have the destiny which is rightfully ours, from Newfoundland to British Columbia.
