subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the hon. member that Newfoundland did join confederation and I was talking about Canadian and not Newfoundland figures.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It does not really matter whether we are talking about eight million people, 800,000 people, 80,000 or eight people in Newfoundland who are unemployed and who find difficulty. The point is that no one on either side of this House has the slightest reason to rejoice when there are unemployed people in Canada. Therefore, I do not think our intent or either side of this House differs greatly.
It rather appalled me that the only constructive criticism I have heard so far today on this subject has come from the government side of the House and not from the opposition side; yet it seems to me the opposition should be the ones to criticize constructively. So I would like to add my little bit of criticism, after saying that I must agree with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) that much has been done since the last time we had a bad unemployment problem in this country. Much has been done to make this grievous problem less grievous for those who are suffering from it. But much more must be done and we must reach the time when we do not have unemployment at all.
For a moment I would like to consider the country as a whole and ask, as one who comes from a non-central province, are the dice loaded in this confederation of ours? I think they are. I think the central provinces control the House of Commons, and therefore they must control the caucus of any national party that has gained power in the House of Commons. The Fathers of Confederation anticipated this. They supposed they would be able to have the regions represented equally by setting up a Senate to which they would give regional responsibilities. But the Senate does not represent regions, and because Senators are appointed it is very hard for us to convince anyone that the Senate represents anyone at all.
Even if the Senate were truly to represent regions, then the Fathers of Confederation did not allow for western Canada becoming part of confederation later, and we have never had the right number of Senators to represent our region in confederation up until today. So I say there is something wrong in confederation; there is something wrong at the seat of power. The federal government always derives all its power from the centre, because the federal government gets its power solely by representation by population, which cannot help but be

January 18, 1971

detrimental to those living in Manitoba, Newfoundland or anywhere else that is not at the centre.
To solve the problem of unemployment and many other problems, we need constitutional reform. I will not talk tonight about constitutional reform. We also need reform of the rules of the House of Commons, which does not necessarily call for constitutional reform. We are not a unitary state, and it is ludicrous for us to go on into our second century pretending that to embody unitary machinery for our government, which is good enough for Britain which is a unitary state, is good enough for us. It is not good enough for us. We need constitutional reform. But be this as it may, in recent years there has been a new concern for true federalism in Canada and a new concern for the unemployed and the unemployable, as the Minister of Labour pointed out this afternoon. The present government has shown very encouraging signs of heeding this concern in both directions, so that some day Canada may provide equality of opportunity for all its citizens no matter where they live or under what circumstances they happen to have been born. Surely that is the good thing toward which we must always work.
I want to illustrate what I am talking about. I picked up the Globe and Mail of last Friday and found on page 1 two important articles on the subject of pollution. The first article said that the lower Great Lakes and portions of the St. Lawrence River already constitute a serious health hazard, thanks to industrial and human pollution. Canada's share of the clean up costs would be around $211 million, in 1968 dollars. The second article said that rapid urbanization and industrialization will accelerate this trend. Within 30 years, more than half of Canada's population will have become concentrated in the St. Lawrence valley and the lower Fraser River valley. So there will be a very serious pollution problem in two beautiful areas of Canada. Does this have to be so? We as Members of Parliament can do something about it if we really want to.
During the holidays I read Pierre Berton's book "The National Dream". I think it is a very interesting book and I would like to paraphrase one thought in it. He said that before confederation, Canada was a country whose population was trapped in the prison of the St. Lawrence lowlands. Now, 100 years later, does it make any sense to sit idly by while the average Canadian needlessly and mindlessly reimprisons himself in that same St. Lawrence Valley and fouls his prison irrevocably in the process?
It is my contention that the latest budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) will, unwittingly I am sure, add its little contribution to the process of fouling up this prison that is being reconstituted in the St. Lawrence valley. All of us surely must decry this process and the fact that it is continuing. This budget may also tend to add to another form of pollution, which is mind pollution, namely, regional discontent that any thinking person who is interested in Canada as a whole must equally abhor.
Let me tell hon. members why I think this is so. In the minister's budget speech I heard no less than six observa-
The Budget-Mr. Osier
tions and statements indicating his and the government's concern for the principle of equality of opportunity for those living in Canada's various regions. I found, however, that in the specific measures the Minister of Finance proposed, only about a third of them seemed to me to have any direct bearing on the aim of narrowing the regional economic differences which presently exist. Yet it is in regional differences of economic opportunity that the root causes of our present grave unemployment problem are to be found.
Forgive me, Mr. Speaker, for illustrating this statement by being very Manitoban in my approach to the subject. In the latter part of 1969 it became clear that the main impact of the government's anti-inflation policy was being felt in Ontario, British Columbia and the Prairies. There were other problems in other places, but they had been continuous or were consistent. These were the ones that showed up as aberrations at that time. Demand was certainly excessive in Ontario and British Columbia, and the government was right when it attempted to cool things in these two areas. Perhaps adverse results on the Prairies, which might not have derived from this policy, could be blamed on the world wheat glut. Well, today the Prairies are selling wheat again. But when we look at the latest unemployment figures we find that the Prairies, Ontario and B.C., in that order, have experienced the greatest percentage of unemployment increase, compared with the increase in December of last year, of any of the provinces.
The Prairies are trying to diminish their relative dependence upon agriculture. For its part, my own province has made real progress in this direction. Manitoba's figures for 1968 reveal that while agriculture accounted for only $480 million, manufacturing was $1,052 million, and mineral productivity was up to nearly $200 million. This should be a healthy trend, one toward which we are all working and one that we hope to accelerate, but our markets for manufacturing are as follows: Some 37.8 per cent of Manitoba's markets are in the rest of Canada, with Ontario and Quebec together being by far the largest portion of these customers, to the extent of roughly 20 per cent. On the other hand, our foreign markets amount to only 5.5 per cent of our manufactured production. In other words, we depend to a large extent on the very markets that the federal government has been trying to cool, while our manufacturers, unlike those in other places, share only marginally in the benefits of Canada's booming export trade.
But if you look at the corresponding figures for Ontario and Quebec, you find that their manufacturers depend upon sales to the rest of Canada to the tune of a mere 13.2 per cent as compared with our 37.8 per cent, far less than either their domestic consumption or their exports to foreign lands, which together account for some
86.6	per cent of their production. We in Manitoba consign or export only 62 per cent. Thus, Manitoba is far more vitally concerned with prosperity in central Canada than one might at first suspect, and Ontario for its part is far less concerned with the west. Here we see a fundamental

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Osier
change from the days of long ago, and here we see that when you diminish activity in Ontario and British Columbia to fight inflation, Manitoba's prosperity is bound to diminish. Other parts of Canada may have needed deflation last year, but we certainly did not need it in Manitoba.
Now, I should like to look at some population figures for a moment. In 1911, the Prairies had 18.5 per cent of the population of Canada and enjoyed 12.2 per cent of the seats in the House of Commons. In 1931, that figure had gone up to 22.6 per cent and Manitoba enjoyed 22 per cent of the seats in the House of Commons. In 1951, that figure had gone down to 18.1 per cent of the population, with only 18 per cent of the representation in the House of Commons. In 1968, Manitoba had dropped to
16.7	per cent of the population, with only 17 per cent of the representation in the House of Commons. It is quite clear that Manitoba and the Prairies have slowly dropped in relative importance, both in population and representation. This has happened since the mid-1930s, and our net migratory figures back this up. Between 1951 and 1956 Manitoba lost 185 people. From 1956 to 1961 Manitoba lost 4,360 people, and from 1961 to 1966 it lost 28,960. Unofficial figures show that this trend has continued from that point.
These facts reveal that trade links within Canada no longer pull east and west, if you look at this matter from the viewpoint of a westerner. They do not seem to bind the east and west together as they did in days gone by. Canada's trade centres are important, but Manitoba's relative trading position within confederation is diminishing all the time. At one time the population of the Prairies was growing and providing domestic markets for the centre. It grew and provided domestic markets for the centre until the 1930s, but it has been steadily declining as a market in recent years. So has the muscle of the Prairies in the House of Commons been declining. At the same time, the importance of the external market for the central province has been increasing steadily.
Thus my figures show, Ontario may be prospering by exporting goods from Canada, but we are exporting chiefly our unemployment problem. We in Manitoba have been an exporter of people for years. We export them to Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. That is why our seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment is only 4.3 per cent, well below the national average. Our unemployment problem is relatively much less severe than it is in many places, but there is very little consolation in this because the people we might otherwise have available to employ have simply left and swollen the ranks of the unemployed in other parts of Canada. When times are good these people have left Manitoba, they have added to the population problem in Ontario and B.C. and they have contributed to inflation in the areas to which they have moved. Then the federal government has taken antiinflationary measures that inevitably clobber Manitoba and some other provinces as well. Manitoba was clobbered last year as an unintended by-product of federal government concern to keep our exports competitive and to keep inflation from taking hold in central Canada. Now we find when times are not so good, the federal
government comes along with remedies based on total unemployment figures at above 4 per cent, which inevitably benefit chiefly the provinces which caused the trouble in the first place but presently have the highest number of unemployed.
Very few measures proposed in this budget will help to improve Manitoba's relative position in confederation, a position, as I have said, that we have seen slowly being eroded over the last 20 years. Some of those measures will apparently worsen that position. By themselves they are good measures and I will certainly support them, but they show little evidence of truly federal thinking, and federal thinking is required today as never before. One chief objective of a federal state must be to bring into balance the elements that make up the whole. This is the stated objective of the government that is presently in power. We must never forget this objective. To achieve it we must return to our earlier preoccupation with the national axis we have built, the axis that flows east and west. If we fail to do so, we are nothing as a nation. Furthermore, we must deliberately foster policies that will move our surplus population into the west and into the north.
Immediate hope for a change must lie in the activities of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I was glad to hear the minister say that upward of $300 million will be spent in 1971-72. But I would like to know what yardstick will be used to allocate these funds. If unemployment is the sole criterion, the money will evaporate as far as Manitoba and some of the other provinces are concerned, because we have exported our unemployment for years. On the other hand, if the yardstick is to be equitable economic opportunity for all regions, which is the stated objective of this government, we in Manitoba will be able to retain our hope for the future of Manitoba and Canada as a whole. Regional economic expansion, coupled with measures already being taken to get Prairie agriculture on a sound, longterm basis, may then become something that is truly effective as we go into our second century.
I have in mind regional economic expansion, plus rationalization of agriculture. A third vital measure which I propose is a regional stabilization fund. Some machinery must be devised so that monetary and fiscal policy can be regionalized in this federal state, and provincial fiscal policy can then be used for purposes of stabilization. I am heartened to know that various ministers of finance are devoting some thought to this problem. I repeat, some way must be found to stimulate or hold back the economy in a specific region without affecting the Canadian economy across the board.
Dr. Andre Raynauld of the University of Montreal proposed such a scheme some time ago. He is a very respected economist. It would seem to me that the federal government has accepted some of his suggestions, at least in part, by creating a loan fund of $150 million for provincial public works. But by making actual unemployment figures the sole criterion, the government has made it impossible for the fund to contribute to fiscal planning on a regional basis, which is what Dr. Raynauld was

January 18, 1971

talking about in the first place. Yet that is one key element in any progress that Manitoba and several other provinces vitally need.
The prime, long-term objective of this or any other federal government must be to work toward a more equitable distribution of income and employment opportunities in Canada as a whole. We must never forget this fact. I have spoken about Manitoba but no doubt my remarks apply to other areas as well.
I commend the minister for his budget. I hope that his next budget in March and his new tax bill, for that matter, will show more aggression toward the question of regional disparity. Then we shall be able to look forward to a Canada in which it is no longer necessary to turn the St. Lawrence valley and the lower Fraser River into a polluted slum, for then, Mr. Speaker, there will be equality of opportunity for Canadians everywhere, no matter where they may choose to live.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the performance of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) tonight in answering an opposition member's question reminded me of a cartoon in today's paper in which the caption reads, "You will feel better when you are seasonally adjusted". I am sure that the unemployed who are walking the streets do not care if we are talking about actual or seasonally adjusted figures. They know they are unemployed, they know there is some reason for their unemployment, and they know the government is not doing anything to help them.
Canada today is a computerized society in which there is unemployment and underemployment. Apparently, most of our problems are fed into computers and before taking decisions the government consults its computers. It seems that the government is not prepared to ask sociologists what the trouble is in this society; it would rather feed some facts into a computer and try to obtain answers that way. It is high time that people realized our society is being controlled by computerization. Until our people realize this, the situation will not be corrected.
Some who have no knowledge of the matters concerned are trying to bring about change. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development has substantiated the fact that Canada has the worst unemployment figure in the western world. That is nothing to be proud of. Apparently the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says, "It is normal to have unemployment." I suggest that the Prime Minister-who is overseas riding turtles, or whatever it is he is riding-ought to be more concerned about Canada. I am sure that we do not disapprove of an individual's recreation or relaxation. However, we want our Prime Minister to stand up and be counted before the nations of the world. His conduct in going off on a weekend when dynamic questions must be settled in the world, was disgraceful, to say the least, and it is hightime the people of Canada told this government that they want the Prime Minister to stand up and tell the rest of the world where we stand on certain questions.
The Budget-Mr. Skoberg
We may well ask ourselves who has created the long queues across Canada for unemployment insurance benefits. Who has made queues outside soup kitchens the norm? The other day I saw the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on television. He was outside a soup kitchen in Vancouver. No doubt he could tell many stories about what he saw in that city. Other members of this House could also recount what their constituents have told them. As a matter of fact, the day before yesterday I learned of an individual, 50 years old, who worked all his life. Now, because he cannot find employment, he must stand in the soup line. He has raised a family and now he is humiliated and is asking himself what has happened to him in this society. It is high time situations like his were corrected.
We must not do what the Prime Minister is suggesting. He is suggesting that only by creating unemployment can Canada fight the inflation that is besetting it. One man alone cannot create the confusion we see around us. The Prime Minister is surrounded by many people who advise him. I understand that he has his own little hierarchy which operates independently of the cabinet. The people in this hierarchy tell the Prime Minister what he should do.
I cannot for one moment imagine the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey), who spoke this afternoon, really saying what is in his mind, because he merely parroted certain words and phrases. We do not expect the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Lang) or the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) to say, "We are not concerned about people". This makes me wonder whether it is not the Prime Minister's hierarchy that is prepared to do away with the pride and dignity of individual Canadians and to curtail their civil rights, as happened recently.
This afternoon the Minister of Labour suggested to my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), that those who are taking manpower retraining are not effectively shown among the ranks of the unemployed. He tried to suggest, in my opinion, that those who are receiving manpower retraining should not be included among the ranks of the unemployed. Yet I have heard of situations across this country, Mr. Speaker, in which people who tried to obtain manpower retraining were not able to obtain it because they had not been on the labour force for a sufficient number of weeks. In other cases, people were not eligible to be paid relocation costs because they had gone out and obtained jobs on their own. I think these are matters the minister ought to look into.
Only last night the editor of one of the Montreal newspapers called Canada the "the publicipatory" democracy of Mr. Trudeau, and I agree.
According to well-documented figures and facts mentioned this afternoon, it appears that unemployment in this country has increased by 40 per cent since last year. We know that these figures do not necessarily tell the whole truth, because many of the unemployed will not go down to the unemployment insurance offices and be classed among the unemployed; neither will they go to

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Skoberg
offices offering social aid and place themselves in a humiliating position. Many people across this country are parroting the phrase: things could be worse! But I suggest that if one examines the facts he will see that things will be worse. The facts show that they will be worse, and this government has told the House of no plans for making them better.
I now turn to the situation in Saskatchewan. The Liberal Premier of that province makes much of the fact that unemployment on the Prairies, particularly in Saskatchewan, has not increased appreciably. I know that the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, is a personal friend of the Premier of Saskatchewan. I also know that he would like to try to educate the Premier of Saskatchewan. That feeling seems to be mutual as between them.
The Premier of Saskatchewan has suggested that unemployment in his province stands at only 2.5 per cent. The Dominion Burea of Statistics says that it stands at
4.7	per cent. The DBS says that in 1969 only 16,000 persons of the combined work force were unemployed in Saskatchewan, and that in 1970 the figure remained at
16.000.	Yet according to DBS figures, 4.7 per cent of the people were unemployed. The Premier prides himself on his figures; they look good. But the export of unemployed to other parts of the country is nothing to be proud of. I suggest that the Premier of Saskatchewan had better look at the situation across the country so that he may know what it is all about.

That is a truly sarcastic
response. The minister sounds just like a professor-no brains, but all smart talk.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I realize the minister's position. He is a friend of the Premier of Saskatchewan and he wants to protect him in the coming provincial election. Of course, that is not why the minister is worried. He is worried about what may happen in the next federal election. He may face problems of his own in Saskatoon-Humboldt, Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He may even go back to the university.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the leader of the NDP (Mr. Douglas) suggested, he may not be back here. I wish to deal with some of the problems in the province of Saskatchewan. On October 1, 1968, the population of that province was
926.000.	On October 1, 1969, the population was 956,000,

and on October 1, 1970, the population was 933,000. There was a drop in the population in Saskatchewan of 23,000 at a time when there also should have been a normal national increase of 10,000. There are 33,000 people who should be living in Saskatchewan today but who are living elsewhere. This is attributable, mainly, to the Premier of that province and Liberal policy. It is no different in Saskatchewan than it is at the federal level, even though they may like to divorce each other. We have seen that happen. There has been quite a lot of discussion about abortion, and I am sure one applies to the other.
e (8:50 p.m.)
In a four month period, 7,000 people left Saskatchewan. What does this mean? If these 33,000 people had remained in Saskatchewan, it is estimated that the unemployment figure in the province would be in the vicinity of 9 per cent. The Premier of that province was interviewed by Charles King of the Ottawa Citizen on December 11, 1970. Mr. King was on a coast-to-coast expedition to catch the Canadian mood. The Premier was interviewed with regard to the general mood of the province. Mr. Thatcher is quoted in the article as saying as follows:
We had our depression here last year. Now we have the lowest unemployment in the nation-only 2.5 per cent.
The article continues:
Premier Thatcher thinks it is a tragedy that Prime Minister Trudeau doesn't pay more attention to the west if for only selfish political reasons.
I do not know if the minister from Saskatoon-Humboldt is aware of the fact that for selfish political reasons he could swing some of the central Canada wealth to western Canada. We have heard about how much money went into wheat input, but there has not been very much encouragement with regard to most of the province. Mr. Thatcher was asked by Charles King what he planned to do in the future. Mr. Thatcher said it will then be time for someone else with new ideas to take over. Although he had not made up his mind, it may be his last election to fight. The article reads:
"And when I go, it won't be to return to Ottawa or accept a Senate appointment."
I understand the Premier of Saskatchewan receives a federal pension. The article continues:
"I've got 10,000 acres running with cattle, and when the weather gets cold, I can always take a holiday in the south. What more can I ask?"
I ask Premier Thatcher whether he would consider passing a little of the 10,000 acres over to the 33,000 people who found it necessary to leave that province. The time has come to look at the situation to see whether we are really concerned about the population. Are we concerned about co-operating with certain people, or with the people in general? In my opinion, this is not being done. I believe the situation in Saskatchewan also holds true so far as the federal government is concerned. The Thatcher Liberals have not used all the money avail-
January 18, 1971

able for public housing. I do not blame the federal Liberals for this. If there is unemployment in Saskatchewan, and the government has not used all the money that is available, who is to blame for the unemployment in that province?
When do the Thatcher Liberals start planning their winter works program? In the middle of the winter the Saskatchewan government decides what to do. Hon. members know that nothing can be accomplished with planning of that nature. The hon. member who spoke before me was quite concerned about the problems of Manitoba, even though he had some good words for that province. The province of Manitoba started to plan its winter works projects last spring and some are being carried on at the present time. The government of Saskatchewan allocated the grand sum of $15 million for winter works. In Manitoba, $74 million was allocated. If the government of Saskatchewan is trying to create employment in this way, I say that province has the wrong government. I am sure something will be done about this situation at the next provincial election. Some of the announcements made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) and other ministers with regard to establishing new projects were as a result of the pressure put on them by opposition members. Pressure was also applied by many thousands of people in today's bread lines. The government knows there is no way that the announced programs can begin this winter.
There will be a very opportune time before the next federal election to lower the unemployment figure. The government knows that by lowering the unemployment figure they can possibly get back in the good grace of the people of this country. I have confidence that the people of this country will remember the length of time they spent on the unemployment rolls and trying to get a bowl of soup. They will remember when the government brought about unemployment. It has been suggested that the Prime Minister is gearing all these programs for a federal election. The Prime Minister has stated we must now fight the economic ill-unemployment. Why has he waited until now? Not very long ago a businessman told me he would be happy if there were a line of unemployed people stretching from his doorstep to the street so that he could pick who he wanted. I wonder whether the federal government and the Treasury Board are using the same philosophy?
This afternoon the Minister of Labour spoke about people getting together, and gloom and doom. I wonder whether he has talked to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. They claim that law, order and pollution are all top issues. I wonder whether the minister has told them not to preach gloom and doom or we may lose some of the carrots hung out by some corporate enterprises. This is another situation wherein the unemployed are not being considered.
There have been many recent news releases and observations in connection with Information Canada. I do not know whether the government is trying to adopt the philosophy of Canadian National Railways, Canadian Pacific Railway and other companies in connection with
The Budget-Mr. Skoberg
contracting out. Information Canada does not hesitate to unload people with many, many years of government service. One such individual is Mr. Stranks. A newspaper article concerning Mr. Stranks reads as follows:
In the past year Mr. Stranks feels the branch has been cutting back on expenditures and "generally tightening up the operation" to meet Treasury Board edicts that it pay its way-
Mr. Stranks charged that Information Canada was following the government hard line so closely that it was sacrificing talent to its budget goal.
"No computer or accountant can tell you the people, the talents and the experience you will need. It can't evaluate related strengths in various fields."
The computer is trying to take over from human beings who are needed in today's world. There is no consideration whatsoever to social issues. In the nineteenth century there were what were called robber barons. They accumulated everything that they could without any regard for mankind or the social and economic concerns of the society in which they operated. We see this today in the actions of the government. There are robber barons in the transportation system. The president of the Canadian Transport Commission is a typical robber baron. I understand that he has one philosophy with regard to the operation of the Canadian Transport Commission, that is, to do away with anything he considers to be not in the best interests of the fast buck process of the railways. As far as I can figure out, the only criterion under which the CTC is operating now, under the direction of its president, is to make sure of a dollar where-ever you can, without worrying about service to the people.
We saw a typical example of this in connection with the recently announced abandonment of trains 7 and 8. The railway company called it a curtailment because they hoped that by doing so they would avoid having to hold a public hearing. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) told us the other day there would be a public hearing. We shall have to wait and see. But under this proposal about 57 men on the work force will be directly affected. In addition there are whole communities which will no longer be served under the proposed arrangement-communities where the primary source of employment is the railroad. Again, we will find one factor affecting another, one abandonment leading to another right down the line.
Across this country from Newfoundland to Victoria, passenger trains are being abandoned. The Transport Commission and the Minister of Transport himself have initiated research projects in this connection but these projects have not been completed. I am sure that had they been completed they would have shown that some of the abandonments should never have taken place.
I see from a news release that the Minister of Transport the other day announced the automation of the Canadian portion of the world wide ICAO aeronautical,
January 18, 1971

The Budget-Mr. Skoberg
fixed telecommunications network. The report stated in part:
Not only has the adoption of this automated system provided improved message transmission standards, but savings in the order of $500,000 a year have been made by the department through reductions in office space, equipment and personnel.
Again we find arrangements made designed to bring about reductions in the number of personnel employed, without any provision for the social climate in which these people live. Similar considerations apply to the CNR servo centres which are being introduced across the Canadian railway system. My information is that as many as 4,000 jobs will disappear with the implementation of these centres. The plan is proceeding, apparently, without any thought being given to the situation of communities which used to have services provided along the line. Again, workers are being told: You are through, fellows. You have been here for 20 years, but too bad.
Most of us have read about the large amounts of money which have been put into the bilingual program. I am a firm believer in a bilingual program, but it makes no difference whether an individual speaks six languages-if he is unemployed, he is unemployed. Millions of dollars are being spent today on language training, and in the end the people who have been able to take advantage of this training find themselves still unemployed. I agree 100 per cent with the leader of the Creditistes when he said some time ago that the bilingual program should start at the bottom and work up to the top.
There is a need for people who are able to speak two languages in this country, but there is also a need to make this possible under a system from which everyone will benefit. It should not be brought in in an atmosphere where individuals in government departments and elsewhere are more concerned about that program than they are about an employment program. The recent settlement with General Motors is an example. The language issue presented no difficulty when the workers were given job security. When people from coast to coast have the opportunity to work, the rest will work itself out. But this does not appear to be the way in which we now operate in Canada.
On May 4 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) the following question:
In view of the Prime Minister's assurance to Mr. Bourassa of Quebec that he would help him to meet his pledge to create 10,000 new jobs in that province by the end of 1971, can the Prime Minister give a similar assurance to the Premier of Saskatchewan who in 1964 promised that 50,000 new jobs would be created within four years?
Of course, Mr. Speaker, you correctly said "Order, please," as you did today, and the question was ruled out of order. The people of Quebec and Saskatchewan know that political promises of this type can do more harm than anything else to the unity of a nation.
I also note that the Quebec Minister of Labour said recently that the province faces more social unrest and political instability if mounting unemployment there is not checked. A news report states in part:
Asked whether this would mean revolution, he replied: "Well, if you want to put that type of word in my mouth, fine. It leads to revolution, certainly not evolution."
I would ask hon. members to recall what others have said as far as revolution and evolution in that province are concerned. The Quebec Labour Minister recently made the statement I have quoted, that perhaps there could be revolution. But has he been brought up under the provisions of the public order bill which was recently before the House? Not long ago the leader of the Liberal Party in B.C. said there could be blood running in the streets of British Columbia. What are these people saying? When one person tries to warn the government about social and economic problems in the country he is accused of trying to bring about an insurrection. But what is the government really doing about its friends, Liberals, who make the same kind of statements on television and in the press?
I turn from those unfortunate remarks, in my opinion, by the Minister of Labour of Quebec and the leader of the Liberals in British Columbia, to the activities of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who is also concerned about wheat. One special interest of his is retraining. He has tried to chase the farmers off the land so that he can retrain them, I suppose. I am sure this is why the Prime Minister put these two jobs together. The minister has not yet told us how he intends to put to work the farmers who have been chased from the country into the cities, but we know they will have to take on the lowest jobs there are. No better example of his approach could be found than the proposal for a production and grain receipts policy. In a description of these proposals, on page 20, I find under the subheading "Encourage adjustment of farm units to more efficient sizes", the following:
The problem of farm consolidation is one which is not peculiar to the prairie region and which, perhaps, is less critical in this region than in other areas of Canada. It is therefore believed that it would be inappropriate to propose programs for the prairie region to deal with the consolidation issue in advance of the availability of programs to deal with this problem in Canadian agriculture generally. Such a general plan is in preparation.
I can only say that I hope the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, who is responsible for this proposal, will tell the people what it is all about. If he does not tell these people, then they are the ones who will become unemployed. Corporate farming will become consolidated and many more people will join the family of unemployed in this country. I urge the minister not to make a hasty decision with regard to this program, and to take into consideration those people who will be affected.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Sullivan).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is the budget debate I intend to speak about the cost of our medicare program, because if we do not do something to alleviate the cost we will find ourselves unable to afford medicare whether or not we have unemployment. It is to be hoped that this government will take a long, hard look at some of the rampaging costs and questionable services that have arisen as a result of our present health care philosophy. Undoubtedly, much good

January 18, 1971

has been achieved by this government's medicare program, but we must examine whether or not this good is sufficient when we consider the cost.
In 1957, Canada spent 3.23 per cent of the gross national product on health care and occupied third place in health care costs throughout the world. By 1966, Canada was spending 4.55 per cent of the gross national product, passing the United States, New Zealand, Great Britain and Norway, on health care costs. The cost of physicians' services rose from $271 million in 1957 to $605 million in 1966. According to the task force on medical care, in 1970 it is probable that Canadians paid just over $1 billion for physicians' services, out of a total personal health bill of $4.7 billion. If we project this forward to 1980, it is estimated that total costs for health care will be nearly $14 billion, with hospitals taking around $10 billion and physicians' services around $4 billion.
It is our responsibility to see that these costs are controlled without sacrificing our ideal, which must be to provide good medical care to each and every Canadian. Ideally, all Canadians should be protected by a health care program which a truly universal scheme would provide. In some provinces-I am speaking specifically about Ontario

this admirable quality has not been achieved. It is reported that approximately 98 per cent of Ontario's population have health insurance coverage. Some have hospitalization without medical care, and some medical care insurance without hospitalization. Two per cent does not seem very much, but in Ontario it amounts to around 140,000 individuals. If these people fall ill, with hospital beds at $60 to $100 per day and medical and surgical fees as they are, this amounts to a real catastrophe for their families. The people without coverage fall into four main categories. First, minorities in ethnic groups, often with language difficulties who do not understand the necessity for application forms. The complexities of having their premiums subsidized in part or in whole when necessary completely eludes them. The second group comprises youth who want no part of establishment premiums, transient tobacco field workers and various other "travellers" with no fixed addresses. Often these people are in poor health and need more care than the general population. The third group is those people who believe they are covered but when sudden illness strikes find to their horror that they are not. Neglect of the last premium notice, errors in billing, change of address and human forgetfulness account for this group.
The fourth group is the young, newly married couples who are not planning a family and are anticipating good health. To them, the monthly $11 for hospitalization and $11.80 for doctors' bills seems a waste of money. No doubt many of them do not require health care, but an emergency appendectomy or an automobile accident without insurance coverage is a staggering blow to their already meagre resources.
In our examination of our health care philosophy it is hoped that we all remember that it is twofold. We must not only insure people against financial hardship arising out of illness, but it is incumbent upon us to prevent the
The Budget-Mr. Sullivan
illness itself. The degree of our victory over such diseases as typhoid, diphtheria, and in our own time tuberculosis and poliomyelitis, came not from advances in health care schemes designed to pay doctor bills but from our ability to prevent disease.
Setting aside for a moment all of the humanitarian aspects and human suffering caused by illness, let us consider how many dollars and cents can be saved by prevention. Let us take cancer of the lung as an example. It is, as hon. members know, the most common form of cancer in the male. Leading authorities agree that it is 85 to 90 per cent preventable by proper health education to eliminate cigarette smoking. The addicted unbelievers here should carefully reread the report of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on tobacco and cigarette smoking, presented by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Isabelle) in the 1969-70 session. The pamphlet "Smoking and Health" from the Royal College of Physicians of London, England, also emphasizes the importance of prevention of this form of cancer.
Let us suppose the disease is not prevented and for a moment follow the usual course of treatment of a lung cancer patient. First, diagnosis must be made. This usually entails hospitalization, repeated sputum examinations by cystologists, multiple X-ray studies and tomogram studies by radiologists, and a bronchoscopic examination. To decide whether opening the patient's chest is warranted, a lymph gland biopsy under general anaesthetic is carried out. If all is favourable, a few days later removal of the lung or part of it is done. This is a long, difficult procedure. Two or three days or more in intensive care with highly trained nursing care, oxygen, respirators and chest suction, etc., follows the surgery. Massive radiation treatment at great cost, usually with the cobalt bomb, is given before or after surgery, and often both. Recurrences are common and a long lingering decline in a nursing home or hospital is usual. Approximately 5 to 6 per cent of all people with lung cancer survive five years.
Forgetting about each one of these unfortunate patients for a minute, let us consider how many thousands of dollars each one requires for such attention, and with so little to show for it in the final result. It is no wonder vast sums are paid for health care under our present system. As matters are now, the first line of defence is prevention of disease, early intervention and health education, and this lies with the general practitioner. In 1955 there were 9,800 general practitioners in Canada and 4,800 specialists, making a total of 14,600 practising doctors. The population of Canada was 15 million. In 1965 there were 10,000 general practitioners and 9,400 specialists, for a total of 19,400. The population was 19 million. Between 1955 and 1965 the population increased by 18 per cent. In these ten years, the number of specialists increased by 94.6 per cent but the number of general practitioners increased by only 4.1 per cent. These figures demonstrate the increasing lag between population growth and the number of family doctors.
In view of these facts, it is apparent that government spending must be more firmly directed toward producing more general practitioners to keep pace with the increase

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. Sullivan
in population, and away from the expensive post-graduate training for specialists. This is the only way day-today family medical care needs can be satisfied. With each passing year hordes of eager, well trained neurosurgeons, orthopaedic surgeons, internists, neurologists, and so on ad infinitum, finish post-graduate courses, and each year there appears to be less and less need for them. In a country with the population of Canada it is unwise for each and every one of our medical schools to be an assembly-line factory, producing every variety of specialist. Canada simply cannot afford to support these comparatively unnecessary training programs with federal funds. The over-all doctor-population ratio in 1957 was .79 per 1,000 population, and in 1966 it was .86 per 1,000 population. So if the surfeit of specialists could be diverted into general practice, the family doctors who now have too little time to spend on prevention of disease and education of patients would be better able to perform these functions.
A general practitioner who sees anywhere between 30 to 60 patients in his office in one day has little time for health care or education. Since this is of prime importance, it follows that much greater emphasis must be placed upon the development of larger graduating classes to general practitioners. The old-time family doctor on call 24 hours a day, seven days a week-friend, counsellor and father to his patients-is fast becoming a legend of the past. The bell is tolling for the passing of the individual, competitive practice of medicine. The game has become too complex and too complicated. Doctors themselves are recognizing this is a practical way. To provide good grassroots medical care, clinics should be encouraged and geographically scattered to allow easy access to all our people. These should not be large nor burdened down with non-productive administrative personnel.
Basically well trained nurses, laboratory technicians and other paramedical personnel would assist the physician in his work by performing many of the routine tasks. Each clinic would have access to the services of certified specialists when deemed essential by the family doctor. Home care programs by visiting nurses, with house calls being made by doctors when required, could eliminate much unnecessary hospitalization. Hospitals could then devote themselves primarily to the care of the more seriously ill. Non-productive administrative staff that has nothing to do with the actual care of the patient would be trimmed to a minimum. Teaching of doctors and nurses, and whatever training of specialists is necessary, would be carried out at a few large university hospitals.
I shall conclude by quoting the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) who said that local doctors' groups in their discussions and examination of our health care system should keep an eye on duplication of services, should look for ways in which we can take a more balanced approach to health care and should make recommendations regarding more efficient operation of the system, as well as continue to improve the quality of our health care system.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate which I can only term most important under the present circumstances.
I assume that the aim of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) in his last budget was the reduction of unemployment, which has developed into a very serious problem both in Quebec and in the other provinces.
This situation of course is getting more and more critical and people are losing confidence in the government because of the increasing climate of unstability.
Catchy slogans have been dreamed up, such as "just society" and "Quebec at work for 1971".; The government seems to have lost control of this situation, and I must simply recall that in 1968 the number of unemployed was near 300,000 whereas today there are about
600,000.
In spite of the tremendous amounts of credit injected into the economy of various areas, and especially into that of Quebec by the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand), that action apparently was not enough. In fact, we still hear day after day about industries folding up or about substantial reductions in the number of workers in various Canadian industries. Obviously, the injecting capital as was done by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is necessary, but in my opinion it is equally important that the existing industries be protected and I think that the government's hesitation in limiting the import of certain goods that we produce in Canada accounts for the closing down of a certain number of plants and for the substantial reduction in personnel.
Several members have spoken before me and they all have quoted statistics which are becoming more and more tedious to listen to. I think that during this debate it is not enough that we should know what is happening. It is also our duty to submit suggestions liable to promote government action and this, not only in order to regain the confidence of the Canadian people, but to provide jobs for an impressive number of unemployed. We are all

January 18, 1971

committed to seeking the solutions they need to earn their living honourably.
Of course, this could be an opportunity to express only strict criticisms of the government. I still believe it to be the duty of all members to seek solutions. The government, if it shows a minimum of broad-mindedness, could accept good suggestions in order to improve this increasingly critical situation.
I cannot help mentioning the situation prevailing in Quebec.
I imagine that other hon. members will take the liberty of discussing what they are most interested in, that is the provinces they represent. As a member from Quebec, I cannot refrain from deploring the present situation in that province.
No doubt the recent budget is very acceptable to Quebec, since an important part of the funds provided will be available to that province, but one must not believe that such injections of capital into Quebec will, in the short run, correct the situation. One must be sufficiently honest to admit that their effect may be favourably felt next summer. With regard to the present situation, it is enough to refer to a statement that the Quebec premier made only ten days ago admitting his deplorable inability to create 100,000 jobs. In fact, it is the second time that we hear the "song of the 100,000 jobs".
I was very disappointed to learn over the weekend that the development of the Sainte-Scholastique Airport which could create 100,000 jobs will only give employment to 22,000 at the most by 1985, according to the statistics supplied by the civil servants of the province of Quebec. We had been brought to dream of this extraordinary project and the majority of people on the North shore were very happy, as 22,000 jobs is a very acceptable and even necessary thing at the present time in the province of Quebec.
But why was this figure exaggerated to reinforce the slogan of "100,000 jobs"?
I would imagine that all municipalities situated near Sainte-Scholastique and those on the North shore were most satisfied to hear that this project was going to provide 100,000 new jobs. Yet sober statistics indicate that the real number is but 25 per cent of this figure.
In April, last year, we heard another promise of 100,000 jobs. With the pitiful failure that ensued, Premier Bourassa must have been hard-pressed (bourasse) by a great number of newspapermen for a good reason, over the past ten days. So, I ask all members from the province of Quebec to come to the aid of the Quebec government and to make it realize that some help from the federal government is obviously needed. I will not let the Quebec government accuse the federal members of being responsible because this promise is proving to be impracticable.
As I said, that slogan was exaggerated. Some now suggest that it was not a promise but that conditions were dramatized. It was not necessary to make such a
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
promise to dramatize conditions; they were then dramatic enough.
I will make some suggestions, because I said that I would not merely criticize. We could make this government responsible for all the evils which Canada is now experiencing. It would be unfair to do so because some members have shown their goodwill.
Besides hesitation created an atmosphere which further deteriorated the situation. The responsibility of those in power should nonetheless be recognized. As for us, for the last two years and a half we have been trying to make suggestions which more often than not are unfortunately rejected.
We must be realistic and honest enough to recognize that the government is unable to check unemployment at present for several reasons. If unemployment is out of hand, we should be honest enough to admit it. I feel that the people insist that we tell them the truth.
In these circumstances, I believe that the federal government should seriously consider calling together representatives of labours unions, businessmen, industrialists, Boards of Trade, certain service clubs, as well as of provincial governments, in order to discuss this problem.
That meeting has to take place urgently so that a solution may be found. It is obvious that the government does not have a solution, and that it cannot find one.
Thus it has to address itself to experienced people and to let them know that this meeting is called in the interest of industry, of financiers and the government, in short of the whole population.
I trust the businessmen. I trust those who have been active for many years in industry to give advice to the Minister of Finance as well as to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and to hon. members.
Such a meeting would first prove the good will of the government with regard to this problem. Such a meeting would prove to the union members and their leaders, to the business world and the population as a whole that we are in earnest about trying to find a solution once and for all.
We could pretend that the present government, in charge of the future of Canada, has found a solution. While the Canadian people waited, it was realized that the government has not really found a solution, that it should ask for the help of experienced men, of businessmen. It must interest them directly so that we might find again the stability which is absolutely necessary for the survival of Canada and the betterment of its people.
Such a meeting might enable us to find solutions for processing our natural resources, here, on Canadian soil, something our governments seem to have overlooked in years past.
It seems to me that in the last few years the government applied itself to improve social measures when it would have been more urgent to improve conditions for industry. Therefore, it would have been possible to create

January 18, 1971
The Budget-Mr. La Salle
new jobs through research and development of new products.
Now, to turn to another subject, should we seriously consider paying the old age pension at 60? I would not know exactly how many persons of that age would qualify. I believe it would be more profitable first to set up an increased pension for people 60 and over.
With an adequate pension to live on, they would make room for thousands of young workers who are now getting benefits out of social legislation. It is inconceivable that so much energy should be wasted in Canada. It is also important to provide jobs for those who are able to work, in order to be able to pay an adequate pension to those who deserve to take a rest. The government should remember this suggestion.
We should also consider the need for student employment next summer. I have had the opportunity, recently, to ask the minister a question in this regard and he answered that he would make a statement in due time. I suggest that the time has now come. In fact, students are concerned about finding a job next summer and I think that a conscientious government should consider the possibility of providing students with summer employment.
Of course the government could consider apportioning a few million dollars more to this end but I think it is high time to restore a climate of confidence in this country.
We must consider giving all our students the possibility of earning a minimum income during the summer season and the government should set up a work program to be assigned to these youth in various fields and departments. It is too late to wonder about what we are going to do. The government must find a solution so that young people will be able, next summer, to earn enough money to complete their education.
As these new skilled workers are entering the labour market, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce should consider the possibility of creating as many specialized positions as possible.
Everybody must be given an opportunity for education, but it is not less important to create as many new jobs. It seems that this has not been the case so far and that our leaders have not taken due account of this situation.
In taking part in this debate, I take the opportunity to urge the government to come back not to reason, but to a more serious approach to these options, to these suggestions.
We must also seriously consider offering alternatives to all those who will eventually have to give up farming. Willy-nilly, a policy was established; it means dissuasion compelling some farmers to leave the farm. In some cases, when the operation is not profitable, consolidation is necessary to achieve profitability. I would be shortsighted if I asked the government to make sure that all the farmers will keep their farm and get enough subsidies to live on.
However, a minimum of organization is required. A number of operations should remain, provided they prove profitable. Considering such a policy, now more and more common, a government is bound to carry on a program affording those forced to relinquish their land and operations an alternative other than social welfare. Unfortunately, for some years, this is all that could be offered them. I hope that our suggestions will be accepted. We have already been urging the government to a sufficient extent.
As concerns construction, it affects a large part of the labour force in Canada. Again, I beg the government to seriously consider repealing the 11 per cent tax on building materials.
The government should also be invited to study the possibility of granting a rebate on mortgage interests commensurate to the income of the individual contemplating ownership.
Could we not also think of a short-term building policy, of paying a premium to all those who want to buy property within a year or two? Such a measure should be followed by capital investments but how can we contemplate this in view of interest rates now prevailing? How can we launch a short-term building program with monthly rents of $130 to $150? This is why it is most important to eliminate the 11 per cent tax on building materials as it would markedly decrease the price of a house and we should also set up an interest refund policy in proportion to the salary of the would-be buyer of a house.
Since the minister in charge is in the House, I will take advantage of this opportunity to draw his attention to the speculative loans which he permitted in certain regions last fall and which were welcome. These loans enabled the average contractors to benefit from anticipated loans and the small contractors to give jobs to some workers.
I agree that the government could and should normally keep at the disposal of contractors a significant amount of money. On the other hand, with the elimination of this distasteful 11 per cent tax and the adoption of a lower rate of interest, manufacturers of building material and officials of carpenters' and of other trades' associations might be encouraged to increase salaries.
Maybe a meeting between the minister and the representatives of all the construction trades associations should be considered in order to come to a 2 or 3-year agreement. There could also be an agreement on the suspension of the right to strike and the wage freeze. Thus the minister seeing the willingness of the people concerned in the building industry, could accept the provision of additional funds for the creation of a short term construction program.
I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that those suggestions will arouse the attention of the minister. I hope the government will approve such a policy for the good of those who wish to own a house.
I also wish to avail myself of this opportunity to voice vigorous protests to the government for having terminat-

January 18, 1971

ed the winter works program. We already criticized severely the government for that. The abolition of winter works shows more than ever this year what a colossal error was made and how costly it is for most of the areas in Canada. A serious study of the desirability of certain works should have been made. On the other hand, a selective system was essential as to the kind of works and the municipalities as well as the provinces should have been given a certain form of guarantee. Keeping the winter works program as regards certain public services and buildings would have enabled us to cope with unemployment. But as the government did not want to understand anything, we must now recognize that the situation is more critical than ever.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the government to vote credits for the construction of sewage treatment plants in several Canadian municipalities. We want to fight pollution, but what are we doing to help the municipalities build them? As long as we continue to talk pollution, we are wasting our time. The municipalities in need of sewage plants cannot afford them; they are already overburdened with debts. The government should, in conjunction with provincial governments if need be, grant the required funds for the construction of sewage treatment plants and thus fight against pollution while creating new jobs.
I want to remind the Minister of Finance that considering the debts of municipalities, it would be opportune to grant them low-interest loans. Almost all municipalities in Quebec must spend 33 per cent of their budgets just to amortize the interests of existing debts. Large sums of money will have to be appropriated so that these municipalities may redeem their debts at a reasonable interest rate. Whether we like it or not, the way things are going it is unthinkable to let municipalities operate as they do now.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot conclude without a few words about the future of the tobacco industry. I had the opportunity to discuss the matter briefly last week when speaking to an amendment to the crop insurance legislation. I hope that the government will seriously consider the future of the tobacco industry.
I met during the weekend some tobacco producers of my area who represent 90 per cent of Quebec cigarette tobacco producers. There are still more in Ontario. They are already concerned because the government plans to introduce a bill to prohibit all publicity concerning tobacco.
I hope that the government will first pass a legislation to prohibit the entry of drugs in Canada and the use of marijuana. How can we win the people's confidence if there is talk of prohibiting any publicity relating to tobacco, an industry which brings in millions to the Canadian government? So, the mere fact of raising this question leaves people puzzled, and rightly so.
On the one hand, the Minister of Agriculture keeps on, and I commend him for it, investing huge sums in the
The Budget-Mr. A. Lambert improvement of certain tobacco soils in Canada, and, on the other hand, the Minister of National Health and Welfare makes sure to inform all the people that if they keep on smoking, they will die.
Thus, this contradiction will do nothing but widen the credibility gap among the people. Let us therefore be serious and practical; let us not allow drugs into Canada as it is being done right now, and we will then be able to consider seriously, rather than condemning the tobacco industry, undertaking studies to help the people understand better the use of tobacco. There is certainly a lot to do in that connection, and in regard to a number of other products as well.
I venture to think that Parliament, in all honesty, will have the courage to take a stand and show sincerity, if we are to really regain the public's confidence and establish a favourable climate. In this way, all financiers and businessmen will come to trust Parliament again and believe that it is possible to find a solution to the unemployment problem so that we may know better times. I hope that this two-day debate will not have been useless, that the time for words has come to an end and that the government will take some concrete measures for the good of the Canadian people.
The Canadian people will be able to regain confidence in this Parliament, if we tell them the truth and if we take action.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think that it is my duty to take part in this debate in order to offer my co-operation. I call upon the government to apply solutions to the serious problem of unemployment and to all other resulting problems.
This afternoon, I listened very carefully to the speech of the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey). From this speech, I kept in mind three main points.
First, he said that in the banks, there was much money awaiting borrowers. Everybody knows that! I am convinced that those who need it more are more aware of it, because it happens very often that businessmen, industrialists come to Ottawa-as was the case last week-to meet officials in order to avail themselves of certain pieces of legislation to offer bankers guarantees allowing them to borrow money so as to carry on their operations.
Mr. Speaker, we know there is a lot of money around somewhere. Everyone knows that banks have the privilege of coining the nation's credit and that is what we are fighting. We consider that is abnormal. 1 will try to prove that within the few minutes available to me.
Would it not be democratic for the Bank of Canada, the people's bank, to have the power and the duty of coining the nation's credit? What is the nation's credit? In my opinion, the nation's credit is a product of people and of activities of all kinds. It is the product of the work of Canadians, whether they work in construction, in a shoe factory or in a garment industry, whether they are professionals, providing professional services to those who require them, businessmen, industrialists or members of Parliament. In my opinion, a nation's credit is

January 18, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
made up of all their activities and thus we can live in society, making use of goods and services exclusively created by Canadians.
The trust that, as the member for Bellechasse, I may have in society is what makes me call on a tailor, tomorrow, and buy a suit if I need one or to call on a doctor to get medical care. This trust in society is what makes up a nation's credit.
If this is what the credit of a nation really is, why should we let institutions cash in on this credit, this wealth of the people, created by the nation, and then lend it to us at high interest rates? Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REDUCTION OF PASSENGER SERVICE IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REDUCTION OF PASSENGER SERVICE IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a week ago in this chamber I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) to intervene on behalf of northern Ontario to dissuade Canadian National Railways from its callous and ill-advised decision to cancel trains No. 7 and No. 8 which presently provide essential passenger and express service in a part of this nation which the Bishop of Moosonee has called "-Canada's cutting edge". In a letter to the Canadian Transport Commission, the bishop wrote as follows regarding the decision to cancel these trains:
comes as a heavy blow to those who live in the communities along the line as well as to those who try to serve them in varying capacities. These communities may be small, but they do contain people whose only access to the outside world is by rail. If I have learned my history right, the principle upon which the railway was built was to weld Canada into a nation by serving such people in isolation. It is a sad day if we change such a worth-while base to that of economic expediency.
At a time in our history when we are trying to unite our nation, we have a publicly-owned railway eliminating services which are essential for the orderly develop-

ment of our rich natural resources. Federal and provincial governments are offering incentives to industry to locate in slow-growth regions, and meanwhile a heavily subsidized Crown corporation drastically downgrades its services in one of these very regions that governments are trying to help.
On previous occasions this House has heard reference to the Mid-Canada Development Foundation, an organization with a plan for the rational development of Canada's habitable mid-north which is fabulously rich in untapped forest and mineral wealth. Canadian National Railways have encouraged this concept and have acted on the advisory council of the foundation. When you consider how the CNR operates across northern Ontario, and when you witness the poor quality of the service they provide, it is easy to conclude that they are in no way an active participant in the plans and projects to unite and develop Canada.
The CNR, in its defence, argues that profit and loss have dictated their decision; that these trains are money losers and serve no useful purpose. Crews working these trains think otherwise. Despite the downgrading of the service on Nos. 7 and 8 to a single coach in which one cannot even purchase a poor cup of coffee and a stale sandwich, these trains frequently travel filled to capacity, with some passengers having to ride in the baggage car while others are left on windblown station platforms due to lack of space. There is not much room in the baggage cars either, because they carry express, especially perishable goods destined for isolated communities along the line and for shipment further north by air.
The railway company argues, further, that its so-called "Super Continental" will assume the workload of trains Nos. 7 and 8. Those who know consider this to be a very bad joke. From December 1, 1970, to January 8, 1971, the "Super Continental" ran on time only once. Over this short period of time it was late for an accumulated total of 200 hours. This performance clearly points out that had trains 7 and 8 not been operating, there would have been many days when daily service would not have been available in many northern Ontario communities. On some days the "Super" was as much as 16J hours late on its eastward run. If it takes on the work of train No. 8, we may expect it to be a day or more late, in which case this transcontinental service will be reduced to milk run status. Perhaps that is part of CNR's grand design, to downgrade this service as well and at some future time apply for its cancellation also. To some it seems clear that the CNR wants out of the transportation business altogether.
The public attitude to the CNR across northern Ontario is one of anger and disgust, employee morale is at an all-time low, and the service provided ranges from poor to none at all. My constituents have asked for a public inquiry into the situation, but the railway transport committee is not so obliging when the service is only a reduction rather than an absolute cancellation-a neat little game of semantics.
CNR officials were ordered to inform the people of the alternate service to be provided, and they travelled shamefacedly across the north like thieves in the night,
January 18, 1971

avoiding as many people as possible, especially railroaders who know the truth of what is happening. I ask the minister to find some way to launch an inquiry into Canadian National's services across northern Ontario. Perhaps the time has come for a major shake-up of CN's top-level management, because whatever they are doing it has nothing to do with serving the public.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REDUCTION OF PASSENGER SERVICE IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerard Duquet (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REDUCTION OF PASSENGER SERVICE IN NORTHERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate fully the genuine concern and interest of the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) regarding the reduction in rail service in his area. A similar question was raised January 13 by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), and I might add that further representations were directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) and to the Canadian Transport Commission which has responsibility in this subject under the Railway Act. I assure the hon. member that the minister has informed the railway of the representations which were made here in the House.
I think it should be made clear, Mr. Speaker, that the action which the CNR is proposing in this instance, effective February 1, is a reduction of service, not a discontinuance of service. The railway is entitled, subject always to the provisions of section 315 of the Railway Act relative to adequacy and suitability of accommodation, to take care of traffic offering, to effect reductions in service on its own initiative, without the approval of the Canadian Transport Commission. Since approval of the Canadian Transport Commission is not required, there is no requirement for a hearing. The minister dealt with this distinction a year ago, on January 12, 1970, to be exact, when in reply to a question by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) he said:
I have to emphasize that where it is only a reduction in service there is no legal mechanism which can be employed. Where there is a discontinuance the Canadian Transport Commission has indicated it will hold hearings on such discontinuances.
With respect to this particular reduction in service, Canadian National has given assurance that if trains Nos. 7 and 8 are no longer operated, every station now served by those trains will be served on precisely the same basis by trains Nos. 1 and 2.
