WHEAT BOARD-PRODUCTION AND RECEIPTS POLICY-STATEMENT IN BUDGET RESPECTING STABILIZATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 8 I addressed the following question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson):
In view of statements made in the House last week by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board that payments under the grain stabilization plan will not be made until after the end of the crop year, could the minister throw some further light on the statement contained in the budget speech that cash stabilization payments would be made next spring and summer totalling $100 million?
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The minister's answer was:
I checked that statement with the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and he agrees that the statement is fair and reasonable.
Thus I am happy to see the minister in charge of the Wheat Board in his seat tonight and I understand he is going to reply to my representation. I asked the question of the Minister of Finance on December 8 in view of two paragraphs contained in his budget speech which I should also like to place on record. As reported at page 1742 of Hansard, the minister said:
Much of the same stimulus would flow from new government proposals in quite a different area. I refer here to the grain receipts stabilization plan outlined to the House five weeks ago by the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. If that plan is enacted and made applicable to the 1970-71 crop year as recommended, it will involve cash stabilization payments to western farmers next spring and summer totalling over $100 million. This would be the net payment contributed by the government to stabilize 1970-71 receipts. There would, of course, be important offsetting savings in government expenditure by the elimination of the temporary wheat storage payments which have been shown to be an inefficient form of assistance. However, the immediate effect of such a stabilization plan would be to put much needed cash into the hands of the farmers next spring.
The largest part of this flow of cash would go to Saskatchewan, where the provincial economy has been hardest hit by the decline in grain marketings since 1968. Large numbers of farmers in both Alberta and Manitoba, however, would also be helped. Taken together with the much higher grain sales and the prospects for further improvement, this early injection of cash would give a significant boost to the entire Prairie economy.
The immediate impact of the minister's statement in his budget speech was a series of headlines to the effect, "$100 million for western grain farmers". These headlines, of course, ignored the very big "if" in the minister's statement, and I think this was to be anticipated. It was underlined this afternoon by the minister's refusal during the question period to confirm that a basic decision had been taken to proceed with such a program. If he wants to confirm that now, I shall be very happy to hear it. These headlines also ignored the elimination of the temporary wheat storage payments and other expenditure reductions which would be effected as a result of the proposal.
I suggest that the Minister of Finance did a disservice to western Canada by giving the impression that a $100 million gift was going to the Prairie grain farmers. This was sloppy thinking and sloppy drafting. I was concerned about the reference to "payments to western farmers next spring and summer totalling over $100 million" because it implied payments before the end of the crop year on July 31. I suggest that this would be impossible unless some sort of complicated advance system were worked out.
Thus, on December 4, as reported at page 1755 of Hansard, I asked the minister in charge of the Wheat Board the following question:
In view of statements in the budget address last night concerning the grain stabilization proposal, could the minister indicate if it is the intention of the government, on the adoption of such a proposal, to arrange for payments under the stabilization plan to the farmers during the spring months?

January 18, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
The minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal indicates a hope to have a payment made for the current crop year. The final determination of the payment, assuming the legislation required is in place, would of course require figures which can only be final at the end of the crop year so it would likely be made in the fall, but it is envisaged that payment of up to $100 million might be made.
The reference to "might be made" was certainly different from the implication of the remarks of the Minister of Finance in his budget address. I suggest that his budget speech is inconsistent in referring to payments to western farmers next spring and summer totalling over $100 million, in view of the statement of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board that payments would likely be made in the fall. I also suggest that the statement in the budget address was unfair and misleading because it gave the impression that $100 million of new money would be injected into the western economy. This is a false statement, for the reasons I have already indicated.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) is in the difficulty of having to find something to complain and worry about in face of a very good proposal for Prairie agriculture. One must also bear in mind his well-established desire for not saying anything very praiseworthy about anything the government does for this sector.
The proposals which were made in this House in late October were, of course, proposals. They were proposals for the purpose of discussion of detail or principle with the agricultural community. But they did convey a clear indication that if put into force they would involve a payment of approximately $100 million to the Prairie farmers for the current crop year. That is the way the situation still stands. Both me and my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), in answering questions
made it abundantly clear that a number of factors require to be settled before the payment in fact is made. These proposals must become a firm policy statement and, indeed, parts of the proposals very clearly would require legislation for them to be brought into effect. In looking at the question of a stabilization fund we have looked at the possibility that over the long haul it might well be wise to have interim payments in the course of a crop year, rather than have the whole of a possibly large stabilization payment wait for. the end of the year.
Oftentimes the shortest cash position will be in the middle of a crop year, which by definition is falling below the previous five-year average. Since we are in that kind of year this year, it has also occurred to us that would be one possible way to deal with the situation now. But, of course, the "ifs" in this circumstance become much more complicated because we have not only to settle the proposals but we must have the legislation in place in time.
The hon. member's difficulty, of course, in terms of specific questions relates to the fact that he asked me one in one term and the other in different terms. My answer clearly indicated that I was focusing on the issue of the final determination of any final payment and the possibilities and probabilities of the payment being made. It is, of course, both in my mind and in the mind of the Minister of Finance, extremely unlikely that the reaction of the farm community will be such as to stand in the way of our going ahead with these proposals. Indeed, I hope in fairly short order we will come before this House with the firm proposals we hope to put in place and which we see as very greatly benefiting agriculture now and in the years to come.
